classification: Rattle and concussion idiophone: hollow brass rings containing loose metal balls, worn on the thumb and fingers and struck together
communities: Jangam storytellers (Budige / Beda Jangams, Mala Jangams)
Kuruma and Golla Oggu Katha narrators
summary: Andelu are hollow brass rings with small metal balls inside, worn on the thumb and fingers of a storyteller's hand. The Burrakatha narrator clinks them in time while strumming his tambura, and Jangam and Oggu Katha storytellers use them the same way to keep the beat.

about: In Telugu storytelling traditions, andelu are jingling metal rings worn on the hand and used to keep time. English Wikipedia's Burrakatha article describes the main storyteller wearing a metal ring called andelu on his right thumb and holding another ring in his other hand, striking them together as percussion [1]. The folklorist Tirumala Ramachandra, quoted by Prof. S. Gangappa, describes the narrator strumming the tambura with one hand and keeping tala with the other, wearing on his thumb a 'jantara' to which a cloth like a handkerchief is tied; this time-keeping jantara is also called gumbilu or andelu [2].

In general Telugu usage andelu are jingling ankle ornaments: C. P. Brown's dictionary (1903) defines ande as a silver foot ornament filled with small pebbles so that it sounds, worn by women on their ankles [3]. Besides the hand-worn rings described above, the name is also used for the jingling rings fitted at the grip of Kolatam sticks [4].
construction: Musician and writer David Courtney describes Burrakatha andelu as a pair of brass rings (toroids) about one and a half to two inches across. Each ring is hollow but split around the rim, and a number of metal balls inside rattle and ring to give a sound like jingle bells [5].

Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy lists three andelu among the few things a Jangam Katha storyteller needs, together with a tambura, bells for both ankles, two gummeta drums for the accompanists, and three gowns and three headcloths for the troupe [6]. Tirumala Ramachandra's description mentions a piece of cloth tied to the thumb ring [2].

Courtney also notes that andelu are used in rural life on bullock carts, where their steady 'ching, ching, ching' sound is said to keep the bullocks calm and less easily startled by outside noises [5].
playing: The storyteller plays the andelu with the hand that is not strumming the tambura. Courtney describes two techniques: one ring slipped over the left thumb and the other on one or more of the other fingers, the two being struck together; or both rings slipped over the left thumb and struck with the fingers [5]. Gangappa describes the main Burrakatha narrator strumming the tambura on his shoulder while sounding the andelu on the fingers of his left hand and singing to the drone of the tambura [2].

In Jangam Katha, the older form from which Burrakatha grew, the narrator holds the tambura, keeps tala with the andelu on his hand and dances, while two accompanists (vantalu) with gummeta drums slung from their shoulders drum and sing the refrain; when the accompanists take up the song, the narrator waves a handkerchief along with the andelu [6]. Budige Jangam storytellers wear andelu on a finger and tap them against the tambura while plucking its string with the other hand [7][8], and Mala Jangam storytellers strike the gourd of the tambura in time with rings on their hands [9].
In Oggu Katha, after the opening praise of Ujjaini Mahankali and prayers to Ganapati and Sarada, the narrator takes up his finger andelu before beginning the story [10][11].
cultural: Andelu belong to storytelling traditions rooted in devotional communities. The Jangams who told Jangam Kathas were Shaiva devotees [6], and their Jangam Kathas are described as the forerunners of today's Burrakatha [2][8]. An old verse from Dhenuvakonda Venkayya's Virataparvam Jangam Katha, quoted by Gangappa, pictures Jangam performers with sacred ash marks, long gowns and turbans, with gajjelu, muvvalu and andelu jingling on their feet as they dance and strum the tambura [2].

In Oggu Katha, putting on the finger andelu marks the start of the story after the invocations [10]. The narrators are Kuruma and Golla storytellers who tell the stories of their deities Beerappa and Mallanna, and entry into the tradition involves an initiation (Oggu deeksha) at a Shaiva shrine [11].

Burrakatha became a powerful medium of public awareness. It spread patriotic messages during the national movement and was used by the Praja Natya Mandali to rouse people during the Telangana liberation struggle; governments and voluntary organisations have since used it for messages on health, literacy and social problems [2][8].
usage: Andelu are a standard part of Burrakatha in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, where the three-member troupe consists of a narrator with tambura and andelu flanked by two drummers [1][2][12]. They are also used in Jangam Kathas and Budige Jangam storytelling, including in Karimnagar district [6][7][8], in Oggu Katha of Telangana [10], and, according to Courtney, in the less common Sarada Kathalu and other Andhra folk forms [5].
Separate jingling rings called andelu are fixed near the grip of traditional Kolatam sticks, with small bells at the tip, so that the sticks jingle as they are struck [4].

uncertain: Which hand: English Wikipedia places the andelu on the right thumb, while Gangappa and Courtney describe them on the left hand; practice may vary with the performer.

Naming overlaps: andelu also means ankle ornaments (Brown), the Virataparvam verse places andelu on the feet, and a 2018 Language in India paper calls the Burrakatha anklets 'andelu or gajjelu' while calling the hand ring 'gajjelu'. Tirumala Ramachandra (via Gangappa) gives jantara and gumbilu as other names for the thumb rattle.
Number of rings: Mikkilineni lists three andelu in a Jangam storyteller's kit, and Courtney describes a pair; performers may wear several.
No source was found on who makes andelu or on beliefs or rituals specific to them.
The claim about bullock carts comes only from Courtney's article.

classification: Gourd-resonated string instrument on a bamboo stick, sounded with small sticks hung with bells (chordophone)
summary: A three-stringed instrument made from a dried gourd and a bamboo stick and played with little sticks hung with bells, used to accompany tatvalu and devotional songs. Its last known player, Dasari Kondappa of Damaragidda in Narayanpet district, received the Padma Shri in 2024.

about: The Burra Veena (బుర్ర వీణ) is a stringed instrument described as unique to Telangana, made from bamboo, a gourd shell and metal strings [1][5]. It has been called an amalgamation of many stringed instruments and is said to be closely related to the Bhoomi Veena and to the tribal villadi vadyalu, instruments played with a bow string [1][2]. A Telugu account places it in the same family as the ektara and the tambura [3].

Only one player is known today: Dasari Kondappa of Damaragidda village in Narayanpet district, a third-generation Burra Veena player who was awarded the Padma Shri in 2024 as its guardian [5][4]. A 2021 review of the study Mula Dhwani likewise noted that only one person alive could play the Burra Veena [7].
construction: Kondappa makes his own instruments, as his forefathers did, and says one Burra Veena takes about a year to make [1][2][4]. First a mature bottle gourd or pumpkin is chosen, which can take eight months to a year to ripen on the vine, and it is then dried for about two months. The gourd must not crack, because a cracked gourd will not sound [3].

When the gourd has dried its seeds are removed and a straight bamboo stick is fitted into it. A wooden bridge is fixed on the gourd with wax, three iron strings are tied along the stick, and pegs made of mango wood are fitted to the far end of the bamboo so that the strings give different notes [3][1].

The sticks used to sound the strings are made from slivers of bamboo: small bells are tied with wire in a ring onto one bamboo stick, and another stick is fixed to that knot of bells [3]. Kondappa decorates the gourd with white vibhuti and kumkum namam marks [3]. He has said that suitable gourds (he names the ash gourd) have become hard to find, so new instruments are difficult to make [4].
playing: Unlike other veenas, which are played with the fingers, the Burra Veena has to be played with the help of sticks [4]. Kondappa plays it with small tingling bells and treats it like a percussion instrument: his right hand provides the bass and percussion, and his left hand the melody [1][2].

He says he can produce 24 different sounds on it, apart from the ragas, and that people who already play the dakki drum, cymbals or dappu find it easier to learn [2][4]. He performs seated on a mat on the floor, and before beginning a song he bows to the instrument with folded hands [3].
cultural: Kondappa belongs to the Mala Dasari community, a Dalit community described as dependents (ashrita) of the Malas. Mala Dasaris spread Vaishnava devotion, and Kondappa travels with his decorated instrument to the homes of the community he serves [1][3].

The family once made its living through house-to-house rounds, singing with the Burra Veena and collecting grain as alms in an akshaya patra. Kondappa says he gave up these rounds, hurt by people's remarks that he was able-bodied and could work for a living, and began giving stage performances instead [4].

The art is handed down within the family. Kondappa learned to play from his father Venkanna and learned the songs from his elder brother Kondanna; he began playing at sixteen and is now teaching his grandson Bhanuprasad [4]. He has said that whenever he plays he feels a deep connection to his ancestors and a responsibility to keep the art alive for future generations [6]. Professor Manoja of Palamuru University has suggested that caste prejudice is one reason few people have come forward to learn it [1].
His performances end with the name of Govinda, remembering his favourite deity, Sri Venkateswara [3].
usage: The Burra Veena accompanies tatvalu, socio-religious and philosophical songs, which Kondappa sings in Telugu and Kannada as well as Hindi [5][3]. His repertoire also includes songs from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Bhagavad Gita, Satya Harishchandra, Bathukamma songs, the Kalagnana tatvalu of Veerabrahmendra Swamy, kirtanas of Manyamkonda Hanumaddasu, Chenchu kommalu and Dharmanga charitra [2][3][4].

A team led by Professor Jayadhir Tirumala Rao introduced Kondappa to a wider public in 2016. The instrument was shown at the Adya Kala exhibition at the State Art Gallery in Madapur in 2021, and Kondappa has performed in an Indo-French music collaboration in Hyderabad and sung in the background music of the Telugu film Balagam [3].

The instrument is critically endangered. In 2019 The News Minute described Kondappa as the only person in Telangana who could play it; none of his children took up the art, though he says he is ready to teach anyone who wants to learn [1][4].

uncertain: Community name varies: Mala Dasari (The News Minute), Mala Dasari / Danda Dasari (V6 Velugu), Vanne Dasari (Kondappa in Namasthe Telangana).

Kondappa's age and lineage differ between reports: 63 years old (IANS, January 2024), born 1 January 1960 (The Pioneer), 70 years old (V6 Velugu); third generation (IANS, Namasthe Telangana) versus 'over five generations' in the family (Humans of Hyderabad).
Type of gourd: 'gourd' (The News Minute), mature bottle gourd or pumpkin (V6 Velugu), ash gourd (Namasthe Telangana).

Exactly how the belled sticks are used (striking the strings or the gourd, and whether any string is also plucked) is not described in detail in the sources; only 'played with the help of sticks', 'with small tingling bells', and the division of bass/percussion (right hand) and melody (left hand) are reported.

The comparison with the Bhoomi Veena and villadi vadyalu comes from Professor Manoja of Palamuru University (The News Minute) and is repeated by The Pioneer; V6 Velugu's placement in the 'ektara and tambura family' is a description, not evidence that it is an ektara.

Possible relation to the 'kaddi vadyam' (కడ్డీ వాయిద్యం) of Dasari singers: the 1992 Mikkilineni survey describes a veena-like instrument of the Mittula Ayyavarlu/Dasaris of Karimnagar played with two thin sticks, and the Mula Dhwani review says only one or two people can play the kaddi vadyam. Whether this is the same instrument as the Burra Veena was not confirmed, so it is not merged here.
V6 Velugu says the materials are found in the Nallamala forests where the community lives, but Damaragidda is in Narayanpet district; this detail was not used.

classification: Concussion idiophone: a pair of long, carved wooden clappers fitted with ringing metal discs
communities: Village Chekka Bhajana troupes (traditionally young men; women's troupes today)
summary: Chekkalu are the pair of foot-long, carved wooden clappers with ringing metal discs that give Chekka Bhajana its name. Dancers moving in a circle clap them in one hand while singing devotional songs and Ramayana stories, a tradition especially associated with Rayalaseema.

about: Chekka means wood or a piece of wood in Telugu [1], and Chekka Bhajana takes its name from the wooden clappers its dancers play [2]. It is a devotional group dance in which the members move in a circle, singing and playing the clappers in rhythm [3][4].

Telugu Wikipedia describes the Chekka Bhajana clapper as a larger form of the chirutalu used by Harikatha performers [5], and Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy uses both names, chekkalu and chirutalu, for it [3]. Summarising the book Janapada Kalarupam Chekka Bhajana by Dr. Chigicherla Krishna Reddy, a lecturer in Telugu University's folk arts department, Mikkilineni reports that Chekka Bhajana arose in Kadapa district of Rayalaseema and spread across the Telugu country; the evidence given is the gurus' own accounts of its origin and the presence of Chekka Bhajana troupes in every village of the district [3].
construction: Mikkilineni describes the clappers as pieces of wood about a foot long, fitted on both sides with pairs of round iron or brass discs that give a pleasant sound when the clappers are struck in time; the wood is decorated with carving [3]. A 2022 report from Chittoor district similarly describes a pair of wooden instruments about a foot long each, with hollowed-out spaces for bells on each side [2], and TeluguISM describes tala-chekkalu about a forearm's length (muru) long [6].

When the whole troupe plays together, the discs sound as one deep sound at a single pitch, which Mikkilineni says spurs on the singers [3]. Telugu Wikipedia describes the performers holding clappers with brass discs in one hand and shaking them as they play [4].
playing: The players hold the clappers in one hand and strike and shake them in time with the tala while stepping forward and back and turning in a circle. A guru stands in the middle and sings, and the members take up his lines as they play; tabla and flute may accompany them [4]. Everyone must step, turn, stop, jump, sit and rise together, and both the dance and the tala change with every song [3].

Mikkilineni lists many named steps, among them adi adugu, rendu potlu, mudu melika, kulukudu, kuppidugu, padma vyuham and parnasala, taught by the guru one by one. At times the guru stops suddenly and the whole troupe stops with him in silence; these pauses, called nilupulu, show the group's unity and discipline [3].

A performance usually ends with jada kopulu (braid figures). A round, moon-shaped board with holes is hung from a high beam or a tree in the village centre with coloured ropes through the holes; each member holds a rope in the left hand and the clappers in the right, and the dancers weave the ropes into braid patterns such as sada jada, nugaya jada, pachala jada and vala jada while singing. If one person makes a mistake, the braid tangles [3].
cultural: Chekka Bhajana is performed as devotion. Before starting, the troupe worships pictures of the gods, breaks a coconut, and holds their clappers while making a full prostration (sashtanga namaskaram) [3]. Young men who want to learn choose a guru and begin with guru puja, practising strictly at night; a troupe takes about three months to become ready, and each guru teaches in his own style [3].

Songs begin with a prayer to Vighneshwara and include devotional songs, episodes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Bhagavata such as the dialogue of Krishna and the gopikas, songs teaching morals, and ballads such as that of the benefactor Budda Vengala Reddy; members step into the circle to act characters and then rejoin the group [3]. Troupes of twenty to thirty in even numbers, aged about twelve to twenty-five, wear matching headcloths, with some members dressed in women's costume for female roles [3].

In the past many villages had troupes, and farm workers gathered at Rama temples after the day's work to chant Rama's name in Chekka Bhajana; television and cinema later reduced its popularity [4]. Performances take place in leisure time and in dry weather, at festivals, at the weddings of deities, at tirunallu fairs, chariot festivals and jataras [3][6].
usage: The tradition is strongest in Rayalaseema. Chigicherla Krishna Reddy's study, as summarised by Mikkilineni, drew on songs and dance postures collected from bhajana gurus of Pulivendula taluk in Kadapa district, and once a troupe is trained it travels to nearby villages and pilgrimage places [3]. Telugu Wikipedia lists troupe leaders from many villages of Kadapa district [4]. In Chittoor district, a troupe from Kanipakam in Irala mandal led by Mohandas, whose family has practised the art for generations, performs at Vinayaka Chaturthi, Sri Rama Navami and Krishna Jayanti and travels to villages between Tirupati and Aragonda [2].
Chekka Bhajana is also found in north coastal Andhra: Doordarshan's DD Saptagiri broadcast a Chekka Bhajana on Seetarama Vanavasam by the J. Apparao troupe of Vizianagaram [7].

Its survival is a concern. Mikkilineni (1992) wrote that support had declined but that villagers were keeping the art alive and that Telugu University was reviving it through training camps [3]. A 2022 report called it a declining art form that has sometimes been showcased at the Republic Day parade in Delhi, and described a project in Chittoor using Chekka Bhajana songs with new lyrics to teach hygiene in schools [2].

classification: Concussion idiophone: a pair of hand-held wooden clappers (castanets), usually fitted with small metal jingles or finger rings
communities: Chirutala Ramayanam and Chirutala Bhajana troupes of Telangana
summary: Chirutalu are a pair of wooden clappers, often fitted with jingles or finger rings, that a singer clicks in one hand to keep time. Harikatha storytellers and Sankranti Haridasus carry small ones, while village bhajana troupes and Telangana's Chirutala Ramayanam use larger, carved pairs.

about: Chirutalu (also written chiratalu or chidatalu) are hand-held wooden clappers used to keep rhythm in Telugu devotional and narrative performance. Telugu Wikipedia describes them as two small pieces of wood with small bells (gajjelu) attached and rings for the fingers, used mainly by Harikatha performers and bhajana singers [1]. C. P. Brown's Telugu-English Dictionary (1903) explains chirata or chiruta as a piece of wood and also 'a castanet' [2], lists chitikelu as 'castanets' [3], and gives the older word gidigillu as 'castanets, or a kind of rattle', equating it with chiratalu and chitikelu [4].

The instrument comes in different sizes. Harikatha narrators use small chirutalu, while a similar but larger instrument is used in group forms such as Chekka Bhajana [1]. Some Telangana art forms are named after the clappers, such as Chirutala Ramayanam and Chirutala Bhajana [5][6]. Wooden clappers with jingles of this general type are found elsewhere in India under names such as kartal or khartal, and in Maharashtra as chiplya [7].
construction: The basic instrument is a pair of wooden pieces. According to Telugu Wikipedia, small bells (gajjelu) are fixed in the middle of the pieces and each piece has a ring through which the player's fingers pass; when the pair is played, the jingle of the bells mixes pleasantly with the sound of the wood [1].

Larger clappers used by dancing troupes are carved and fitted with metal discs. Describing the clappers of Chekka Bhajana, which the same author also calls chirutalu, Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy records pieces of wood about a foot long, decorated with carving, with two round iron or brass discs fixed on each side so that they ring when struck [8].
playing: Chirutalu are held and clicked in one hand, leaving the performer free to sing, dance or play another instrument. The Harikatha narrator holds chirutalu in his hand and wears ankle bells, singing, narrating, acting and dancing for about three hours, usually accompanied by a violin, veena or harmonium and a mridangam [9][10].

The Sankranti Haridasu strums a tambura on his shoulder and keeps time with chirutalu in the other hand, singing and dancing with bells tied to his ankles as he stops before each house [11]. English-language reports describe the same practice as carrying 'chidathalu' in one hand and a tambura in the other [12][13].

In group forms the whole troupe plays together. In Chirutala Ramayanam, thirty to forty young village labourers plant a pole with flags in an open space outside the village, hold chirutalu, tie bells to their ankles and sing and dance; the author compares it to Kolatam, except that the troupe dances with chirutalu and its members act the roles of Ramayana and Mahabharata stories [5]. In Pandari bhajana the dancers hold chirutalu while singing and miming the songs, accompanied by dholak or maddela, kanjira, tambura, talalu and harmonium [14].
cultural: Chirutalu belong mainly to devotional performance. Mikkilineni describes elderly villagers sitting to sing Hari bhajanas and Pandari bhajanas with hand cymbals and chirutalu, and devotees singing Jayadeva's ashtapadis, Purandaradasa's and Annamacharya's songs with chirutalu, clappers, cymbals, tamburas and ankle bells [15].

The Haridasu's round with tambura and chirutalu is a Dhanurmasam and Sankranti custom. He bathes at dawn, wears saffron cloth, namam marks and garlands, and carries an akshaya patra on his head; when a household offers rice he kneels to receive it and blesses the family [11]. A 2018 Yo! Vizag feature adds that he sings 'Harilo Ranga Hari' and Ramadasu's kirtanas, is said never to stop to ask for alms or look back, and that villagers wash his feet and seek his blessing [12].

Group troupes learn from a guru. Chirutala Ramayanam troupes engage a guru to teach them during the summer [5], and before a Chekka Bhajana performance the troupe worships pictures of the gods, breaks a coconut, and holds their chirutalu while prostrating before they begin [8].
usage: Harikatha, the solo musical storytelling form that Adibhatla Narayana Dasu shaped into a distinctive art, is performed at night, especially during Ganapati Navaratri, Dasara, Krishna Jayanti, Mukkoti Ekadasi and Sankranti; long Ramayana, Mahabharata or Bhagavata series can run for fifteen days to a month [9].

Haridasus singing from house to house with chirutalu appear in Telugu villages and towns during Dhanurmasam, the month leading up to Sankranti, and are otherwise rarely seen during the year [11]. A 2020 BBC News Telugu report described the Haridasu as a tradition that is disappearing in modern times [13].

Chirutala Ramayanam is widespread in Telangana and described as a very old form in Karimnagar district. Mikkilineni (1992) notes that its popularity fell after cinema arrived but that troupes were still active in villages such as Thotapalli, Cherla Buthkur, Chintakunta and Veenavanka [5]. Recent Telugu television news reports show Chirutala Ramayanam performances in Karimnagar district in 2026 and an eight-hour non-stop Chirutala Bhajana performance there in 2025 aimed at a record [16][6].

Chirutalu are also used in Pandari bhajana, a dance-centred bhajana that came from Maharashtra and in which children take part in large numbers [14], and a Chirutala Bhajana troupe took part in the cultural procession held in Hyderabad on 17 September 2022 for the Telangana Jateeya Samaikyatha Vajrotsavalu celebrations [1].

uncertain: English-language sources often call these clappers 'cymbals' (for example Yo! Vizag's 'chidathalu (cymbals)' and English Wikipedia's Harikatha article, which says the storyteller uses 'a pair of cymbals'), whereas Telugu Wikipedia and Brown's dictionary describe wooden clappers or castanets. Some narrators may use small cymbals instead; this could not be settled from the sources.

Spelling varies: చిరుతలు (Telugu Wikipedia, Mikkilineni), చిరతలు (Mikkilineni's Harikatha chapter, S. Gangappa) and చిడతలు (BBC News Telugu). In everyday Telugu చిటిక/చిటికెలు also means a finger snap, so 'chitikelu' is ambiguous; Brown (1903) is the only source found that uses it for castanets.

The word chirutalu is used loosely: Mikkilineni also calls Kolatam sticks 'kolatapu chirutalu' and the Chekka Bhajana clappers 'chirutalu'. The large carved clappers of Telangana's Chirutala Bhajana appear to be the same kind of instrument as the chekkalu of Chekka Bhajana, which are described in a separate file (chekkalu.json).
No source was found on who makes chirutalu, what woods are used for the small Harikatha type, or making rituals specific to the instrument.
The list of active Chirutala Ramayanam villages comes from a 1992 book and may be out of date. The 2025 and 2026 news reports were known only from their titles and short descriptions.

classification: Frame drum (single-headed membranophone), played with two sticks
summary: A large, flat, one-sided frame drum beaten with two sticks, made and played for generations mainly by the Madiga community. It sounds at weddings, goddess festivals, processions, village announcements and funerals, and has become a symbol of Dalit pride and protest.

about: The dappu (డప్పు) is a flat, round frame drum with a skin stretched over one side, beaten with two sticks; C. P. Brown's Telugu-English Dictionary (1903) simply calls it 'a large drum' and a drummer a dappuvadu. [11][1][7] It is closely tied to the Madiga community of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, who have historically both made and played it, and Firstpost notes that every celebration in a Madiga household begins with the family playing the drum and dancing. [1][2]

Its beat is part of almost every public occasion in the Telugu countryside: weddings, festivals of village goddesses, jataras, processions and funerals. For generations a drummer walking through the village has also been the way to announce news, from the sale of goods to a panchayat meeting, a practice called chatimpu or dandora. [1][3][5][7]

The drum has several regional names. Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy's survey of Telugu folk arts says dappu drumming is also called tappetla vayidyam, and that in Rayalaseema the drums are called kanaka tappetlu. [5] Firstpost reports that the circular wooden frame is called gundu in Telangana and palaka in Andhra Pradesh, and Telugu Wikipedia adds that in some areas the whole drum is called palaka. [1][8] Similar frame drums are known as thappu or parai in Tamil Nadu. [1]

A village saying quoted by Madiga elders sums up its place in life: 'Penli ayina chavu ayina, dappu debba padilsinde' (పెళ్లైనా, చావైనా డప్పుదెబ్బ పడాల్సిందే) - whether it is a wedding or a death, the dappu must be struck. [1][8]
construction: The frame is a ring of wood, usually neem or tamarind; Mikkilineni names neem and chandra wood. [1][2][3][5] The head is animal hide. Sources mention calf skin, the skin of a young male buffalo or goat, and more generally the hides of cattle, buffalo or goats. [5][7][1][3]

Making a dappu is slow, careful work. The hide is tanned, treated with ash and salt so that it does not rot, and dried. It is then pasted onto the wooden ring with a thin, sticky paste made from tamarind seeds and the bark of tangedu (Tanner's cassia), tied tight with string and left under a weight. [2][1] An elderly cobbler interviewed by Firstpost explained that thicker skins went into sandal soles and thinner ones into dappus. [1]

Fire is part of both making and playing the drum. Once the skin is fixed, the dappu is exposed to fire so that loose edges pull tight. [1][2] Drummers warm the head over a flame before playing so that it gives a bright ringing sound, which Mikkilineni describes as 'kanakana'; The Hindu describes drummers at a night performance warming their dappus in the glow of a bonfire, the skin going taut in the heat. [5][4][10]

Firstpost reports that dappus were sold only in small shops owned by Madigas, because mainstream music shops that sell other leather instruments would not stock them. As Madigas lost access to hides, drums with synthetic or plastic heads became common, especially in towns. [1][2]
playing: The drummer carries the dappu slung from the shoulder and beats it with two sticks. [3] The short, thick stick in the right hand, called sirra or sirre, strikes the lower part of the head and creates the rhythm; the long, thin stick in the left hand, called sittikenna pulla (or chitikena pulla), plays near the upper side and controls the pace. [1][7] Skilled drummers change the sound further by resting the left palm on the upper rim. [7] The News Minute calls the pair of sticks 'chirra-chitike'. [2]

Each occasion has its own drumming style (debba or daruvu): the beat for a wedding procession is different from the beat for a festival of the gods, and the beat played when someone dies is different again. [5][7] A 2021 training course in Hyderabad taught learners at least ten popular jatis (beats) and the human pyramids that dappu troupes build while playing. [3]

Dappu dance is done by troupes of about ten to twenty drummers wearing ankle bells, often at the head of a procession. It opens with a slow circular invocation called pradhana dappu and uses named steps (adugu) such as ata dappu, okka sira dappu, samidika dappu, madil dappu and gundam dappu. [7] In dappula kolatam the dancers hold the drums under the arm and strike each other's sticks as in a stick dance while leaping with belled feet. [5]

Mikkilineni records virtuoso tricks from weddings in Nizamabad district, where the number of dappus in a wedding procession is a matter of prestige: a drummer plays so that the vibration knocks coins off an upturned dappu on the ground, or picks up currency notes from the ground with his eyelids without losing the rhythm. He also notes that Amrutayya of Kanumuru and Yesu Dasu of Unguturu in Krishna district played mridangam patterns on the dappu and toured with the Praja Natya Mandali. [5]
cultural: Madiga oral tradition tells several stories about how the dappu began. In one, a hunter who accidentally killed a female monkey took home the flat drum her mate had been playing, and his village learnt to play and make it. In another, a man kicked a stone onto a dried hide and its sound frightened away wild animals; folklore also calls the dappu the first instrument early humans made to announce their presence. The oral epics Jambava Puranam, Dakkali Puranam and Baindla Puranam give further accounts of its origin. [1][2]

By custom the dappu was played only by men, while women joined in the dancing and singing. In recent years some women, among them the singer and activist Vimalakka, have taken up the drum, though this is still not common. [1]

Because it is made of leather by Madigas, dominant castes treated the dappu as an 'untouchable' instrument, and some Madigas stopped making or playing it out of fear of shame. [1][2] Dappu artist and documentary filmmaker Lelle Suresh answers this prejudice with the words: 'When a cow is holy, its skin can't be unholy.' [2]

From the 1980s the drum became a symbol of Dalit self-respect. After the Karamchedu (1985) and Tsundur (1991) massacres, artists such as Kalekuri Prasad sang about these events to its beat, and the campaign for sub-classification of Scheduled Caste reservations that began in 1994 took the name Madiga Dandora, after the drum-beaten announcement, with 'cheppu-dappu' (sandal and drum) as its emblems of dignity. [1][2] Revolutionary cultural troupes such as the Jana Natya Mandali and singers like Gaddar made the dappu central to their performances. [7][1]
usage: The dappu accompanies weddings, festivals of folk goddesses, jataras, car festivals of deities, worship of veerulu (hero deities), Veerabhadra performances and funerals across Telugu villages. [3][5][7] During Bonalu in Hyderabad, dappu beats resound in the processions in which Potharaju dances ahead of the goddess's offerings. [9]

It is the main instrument of dappu dance and dappula kolatam, and Firstpost notes that the Chindu dance evolved alongside it. [5][1] In Telangana, Mikkilineni describes the Jogu people, a Dalit sub-group, dancing with dappus at weddings and festivals and also while carrying their dead to the cremation ground. [6]

The drum has powered mass movements on Telugu soil: Naxalite and Maoist cultural troupes, Dalit movements and the public meetings of the Telangana statehood movement all relied on dappu artists, and political parties of every colour now bring dappu troupes to their rallies. [2][3]

Artists and scholars say the art has been undervalued. PhD scholar Andey Bhaskar points out that no dappu artist has been nominated for honours such as the Padma Shri, and in March 2021 the Telangana Department of Language and Culture ran a 15-day dappu training programme in Hyderabad for about fifty learners, including four women, to revive the form. [2][3]

uncertain: Size is not agreed: P. Kesava Kumar gives the frame a radius of about six to eight inches, while Telugu Wikipedia says the drum is about two feet across. Sizes probably vary, but no measured description was found. [7][8]

The name palaka: Firstpost uses it for the wooden frame in Andhra Pradesh, Telugu Wikipedia for the whole drum in some areas. A popular website also lists names such as Koya, Thappeta, Kanaka Thappeta and Tikora and explains 'palaka' by a resemblance to a duck; only tappeta and kanaka tappetlu could be confirmed from a second source (Mikkilineni). [1][8][12][5]

Firstpost says the skin is 'processed with chalk and tangerine wood'. This is probably a mistranslation of tangedu (Tanner's cassia) bark, which The News Minute names; this page follows The News Minute. [1][2]

Firstpost states that only Madigas play the dappu. Other sources show related use by other groups: Mikkilineni describes the Jogu of Telangana dancing with dappus, and his chapter on tribal instruments says the Raj Gonds of Adilabad play a similar frame drum (the tapna) with two sticks named dappu and dang. Whether all these are the same instrument was not established. [1][6][13]
Heating the skin over a fire before and during performances is described by several sources, but none describes a fixed ritual or rule around it (for example a puja before heating).
Telugu Wikipedia says the dappu is used in Chindu Bhagavatam; this was not confirmed in another source consulted. [8]
The number of named rhythms is not settled: one popular website speaks of about 30 daruvus, while a government training course taught ten. [12][3]
The AIF article (a photo essay about the Prajwala Sangham in Hyderabad) has no visible publication date.

classification: Double-headed barrel drum (membranophone)
communities: Hereditary nadaswaram and dolu (mangala vadyam) musicians

summary: A barrel drum with skins on both ends. It is the rhythm partner of the nadaswaram (sannayi) in the auspicious mangala vadyam music of weddings and temples, and it is also the big drum of Telangana's Oggu Dolu dance, the Koya Kommu Koya dance and many rituals and processions.

about: Dolu (డోలు) is a general Telugu word for a drum. Dictionaries define it as a charma vadyam (an instrument sounded on a stretched skin) and trace it to Sanskrit ḍhōla, and old poetry names it alongside other instruments, as in a verse of the Accha Telugu Ramayanam quoted in the Sabdaratnakaram that lists bheri, dolu, tappeta, kale, flutes and tudumu together. [1]

In the classical mangala vadyam (auspicious music) of South India, the dolu is the drum that accompanies the nadaswaram, which in Andhra is called sannayi. Dolu artist and Telugu scholar Dr. Bhusurapalli Venkateswarlu writes that the same drum is called tavil in the Tamil region, that old musical treatises called it shringabheri or dindima, and that it is said to derive from Shiva's damaru. [2]

In folk and tribal traditions the name covers other large barrel drums, such as the brass Oggu dolu of the Kuruma and Golla communities of Telangana and the drums worn by Koya men in the Kommu Koya dance, which is also called Kommu dolu. The Telugu Akademi's regional dialect dictionary (2004) also records dolu as the Telangana dialect word for the drum called ḍhaṅkā, which is tudumu in the North Coastal Andhra (Kalinga) dialect. [3][4][1]
construction: Bhusurapalli Venkateswarlu describes the dolu of the nadaswaram ensemble as closed with skin on both sides, one side played with the hand and the other with a stick about a foot long. [2]

M. A. Rauf's account of tribal instruments, reproduced by Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy, describes the tribal dolu as a hollowed wooden body with deer skin or goat skin on both ends, kept taut with pieces of bamboo and ropes. [5]

The Oggu dolu of Telangana is about a metre long and drum-shaped. Mikkilineni writes that it is now made of brass but was formerly made of wood, with goat skin fitted on both sides and tightened with ropes, and that it gives a deep, resonant sound. It is beaten with sticks of jilledu (calotropis) or custard-apple wood. Similar drums in Kurnool and Anantapur districts of Rayalaseema are called Veerappa dolla. [3]
playing: A mangala vadyam group (melam) has two nadaswarams, two dolus, a drone (sruti) and cymbals (talam), and a nadaswaram concert opens with the dolu. Bhusurapalli argues that because two dolu players both cooperate and compete in every concert, dolu playing developed far more elaborate counting and rhythmic patterns than other skin drums. [2]

Rauf describes a second kind of tribal dolu that is hung from the neck with the drum resting against the belly, and struck with a bamboo stick in one hand and the fingers, sometimes the palm, of the other. In the Kommu Koya dance, men wear a large dolu from the neck and play it in rhythm while stepping in a circle in the dance called Permichor. [5][4]

Oggu dolu players dance in circles while drumming vigorous patterns and perform feats: holding the drum's ropes in their teeth while they dance and play, or sitting with the drum against the back and playing it with their arms turned behind them. [3]
cultural: The mangala vadyam is inseparable from Hindu weddings and temple worship. Bhusurapalli writes that as soon as the turmeric root is broken for a wedding in a Hindu home, the mangala vadyam must sound, and that the 'tom tom tom' with which the dolu opens a nadaswaram performance recalls the Omkara of Shiva's damaru. [2]

The Kurumas and Gollas regard the Oggu dolu as a mangala vadyam at weddings. Seven or eight dolus are played together at goddess-temple festivals, at jataras and during worship in Shiva temples, and the drum is played at Mallanna festivals and processions and at rites such as going to the water (jaladhi), mailapolu, nagavalli and veerabonam. Before an Oggu Katha the dolu is sounded as a signal, and the whole village gathers at its sound. [3]

In the Veerabhadra festivals of Veerashaiva devotees, dolus beaten at great speed, together with a special instrument called veerangam, sannayis and conches, drive the ecstatic sword-bearers and the devotees who pierce their tongues with skewers (narasalu). In Veeranatyam, the dance of the Veerakumarulu is spurred on by sannayi, dolu, tambura and tasha. [6][7]
For the Koyas, the dolu dance is performed at Bhumi Puja, the first-harvest festival, and at life events from birth to death. [4]
usage: As part of the mangala vadyam the dolu is played at weddings, in temples and at festivals throughout Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Bhusurapalli names first-generation Telugu dolu players such as Penugudurupadu Ankamma, Modukuri Balakotayya, Kuntupalli Guravayya, Parella Ammisetti and Turumella Subbarayudu; later players in the Thanjavur style such as Annavarapu Basavayya and Emani Raghavayya; Tirupati Muniramayya; and Layabrahma Bhusurapalli Adiseshayya, Nidamanuri Lakshminarayana, Vijayawada Kannarao, Munnangi Venkateswarlu and Tarigopula Narayana, noting that their families have lived by the art for generations. [2]

In folk performance, three players with dolu, cymbals and kanjira stand behind the storytellers of Oggu Katha, and Mikkilineni describes big dolus in the Golla suddulu storytelling and among Telangana's Yadava storytellers. The dolu and a sruti sannayi accompany the Gangireddu (decorated bull) performers, Dommara acrobats beat their dolu to gather the village before a show, and the Mala Jangalu count the dolu among their best-known instruments. [3][8][9][10][11]

In January 2026, 30 Oggu Dolu artists from Jangaon, Siddipet, Vikarabad, Jagtial, Peddapalli and Sircilla districts, led by Dr. Oggu Ravi, were selected to perform on Kartavya Path in the Republic Day parade, the first time the art form was included. [12]

Writing in 2006, Bhusurapalli warned that under the din of foreign instruments, nadaswaram and dolu music was surviving 'with its last breath' and the livelihood of young players had become uncertain, and he appealed to the government and cultural bodies to support these musicians. [2]

Bhusurapalli's statement that the dolu derives from Shiva's damaru is a traditional view, not a documented history.

The Oggu dolu is closely tied to Oggu Katha; if the Oggu page also covers the Oggu dolu, the two pages should be cross-checked. Mikkilineni's statement that it is 'about a metre long' and now made of brass is from 1992 and may not apply to every troupe.

Sources often associate nadaswaram and dolu playing with particular hereditary communities, but the sources read for this page (Bhusurapalli) speak only of hereditary families, so no caste is named here.
Some sources describe the Koya drum as a large cowhide drum; the material of the Koya dolu was not confirmed in the sources read.

classification: Single-headed clay pot drum (membranophone)
summary: An earthen drum of the Raj Gonds of the Adilabad region, bought from local potters and covered with goat skin. Played in pairs with the palm, it has a soft, mellow tone and accompanies the dance songs of the Dandari festival season before Diwali.

about: The gumela (also written gummela or ghumela) is a clay drum played by the Raj Gonds of the Adilabad region of northern Telangana, above all during the Dandari festival season that leads up to Diwali [1][2][3]. The anthropologist Christoph von Fürer-Haimendorf, writing in 1948, described gumela as bulbous 'bottle-drums' of burnt clay with a single membrane over the open base, and noted their 'extremely soft tone' [1].

It is one of the core Dandari instruments. With the parra and vette drums it is worshipped at the start of the festival and stored away again at its end, and newspaper and other accounts list it among the instruments heard during the Dandari–Gussadi celebrations [2][4][5][7].
construction: The body of the gumela is made of potter's clay and is hollow inside [1][6]. Haimendorf reported that the Gonds ordered their gumela drums from Telugu potters; the traditional payment for a pair of drums was one fowl and one or two seers of rice, and by the 1940s buyers gave the potter a chicken, some grain and often cash as well [1].

A goat-skin membrane is stretched over the open end. Haimendorf wrote that the membranes are attached with iron hoops and leather thongs, and his drawing shows a gumela with a flask-shaped body of potter's clay and a membrane of goat hide [1]. The Telugu writer Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy, drawing on M. A. Rauf's survey of tribal instruments, describes the gumela as made of potter's clay, hollow, cylindrical in shape and tightly covered with goat skin [6].
playing: Gumela are always played in pairs. The player beats the membrane with the palm of the right hand, while the left hand alternately opens and closes the narrow neck of the drum [1].

The sound is soft and mellow. Haimendorf described young people in the rainy season dancing at night 'to the mellow tone of the earthen gumela drums or the small handy para, beaten caressingly with gentle fingers', and contrasted the melodious gumela dances with the livelier dances accompanied by the para drum [1].

In the Dandari ensemble each pair of gumela goes with one or two vette (turbuli) drums [1]. Haimendorf saw young men carry gumela drums with a visiting Dandari troupe, and his photographs include gumela players accompanying the Dandari dancing [1].
cultural: Owning Dandari drums was traditionally a matter of inherited right. Haimendorf reported that anyone may play them, but only men with a hereditary right could own gumela or para drums. Tradition said that gumela were first owned only by men of the four-brother clans and later also by the seven-brother clans, although by the 1940s men of any phratry owned them, and he knew of no man who owned both a para and gumela [1].

A legend recited by the Pardhan bards, known to most Gonds, tells how the ancestor Dundria Raur and Manko (now revered as a deity) began the making of dance drums and the custom of Dandari troupes visiting friendly villages; in it the gumela are brought by the four-brother clans from Bamni. Because of this legend, Gonds see Dandari dancing as a religious duty as well as entertainment, and they revere Dundria Raur and his brother Sipiserma Raur as dance gods (Yetmasar Pen) [1].

A new gumela must be consecrated before it is played. No ceremony is needed while the drum is being made, but before its first playing a chicken is sacrificed in honour of Dundria Raur, patron of dance and song, and the drum must be touched by a menstruating woman. The new drums are laid on a white cloth behind a screen, sprinkled with water, vermilion and turmeric and then with the chicken's blood; afterwards the owner and the dancers each spin on one heel over a peg driven into the ground where the offerings are buried, which is believed to give swiftness and vigour in dancing [1].

At the start of the Dandari festival, on Bhogi day, the gummela is worshipped together with the parra and vette drums and the kodal dance sticks before the Gussadi costumes are put on [4]. At the closing Kolabodi rite the Dandari instruments are taken to the mahua tree of the god Chenchi Bhimanna outside the village, sacrifices and worship are offered before them, and drums such as the gumela, parra and vette are then put away until the next Akadi festival [7].
usage: The gumela is played during the Dandari season: Haimendorf recorded that the dance drums are taken out after the Akadi rite and may then be played every night until the end of Dandari, when troupes of young men travel to friendly villages to dance [1][7].

Gumela songs are dance songs. Haimendorf found that many simply list the gods worshipped, the crops in a man's field or the ornaments worn by a beautiful girl, while others sketch a meeting between a boy and a girl; in one such song a girl is teased with the words 'waist like a gumela' [1]. Boys also gathered round fires at night with para and gumela drums before the first-fruits rite (Nowon), singing songs that listed the vegetables they were not yet allowed to eat [1].

The Dandari–Gussadi festival is celebrated in tribal villages of Adilabad and Kumuram Bheem Asifabad districts and parts of Mancherial and Nirmal districts. During the festival the Gonds revere the goddess Jangubai by playing instruments before her, and the ghumela is named among the instruments used, together with the dappu, dhol, vette, karra and tudum [2][5].
In 2021 The Hans India reported that these Dandari instruments were almost extinct from the markets and that some tribal groups were starting to use DJ sound systems during the festival [2].

Kolams also celebrate Dandari, and a drum labelled 'Kolami Gumela' is displayed at the Kumuram Bheem Tribal Museum, Jodeghat (according to its Wikimedia Commons description), but no written source confirming Kolam use of the gumela was found.
The ownership rules and the payment to potters are from Haimendorf's fieldwork in the 1940s; present-day practice was not confirmed.
The English Wikipedia table of Gussadi instruments ('a drum made of clay and animal skin') gives no citation.
The name is close to the Telugu clay drum gummeta, and Haimendorf says Gonds bought gumela from Telugu potters; whether the two are the same instrument type was not researched here.

classification: Single-headed pot (goblet) drum with an open end (membranophone)
summary: A small pot-shaped drum with a skin over one end and an open mouth at the other. The two side-singers of Burrakatha (Jangam katha) hang it from the shoulder and strike the skin with their fingers while the other hand opens and closes the mouth to change the sound.

about: The gummeta is the drum of the Burrakatha storytelling tradition. Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy writes that the Jangam storytellers are also called Budige Jangalu after the instrument they use in their stories, the budige, which is known in different regions as dakki, dikki or gummeta. Among the art's many names are gummetla katha and dakki katha, and Mikkilineni reports a view that even the name Burrakatha comes from 'burra', said to be another name for the gummeta, alongside the explanation that it refers to the gourd resonator (burra) of the storyteller's tambura. [1][2][3]

Telugu dictionaries describe the gummeta as a kumbha vadyam (pot drum) and as a small drum. Vavilla's dictionary (1949) quotes Krishnadevaraya's Amuktamalyada, where the gummeta appears in a long list of instruments, and C. P. Brown's dictionary (1903) also cites the word from classical poetry. [4][5][6]

The word is Dravidian: the Dravidian Etymological Dictionary lists Telugu gummeṭa and gummeta ('a kind of small drum') together with Tamil kummaṭṭam ('a small drum') and Gondi gumela ('kind of drum'). The Purushottama Kaviyamu (1918) instead derives it from Sanskrit gumbhita. [7][4]

Mikkilineni reports the view of scholars that the veeragumbhita drum, played by a woman while a heroic ballad is sung in the medieval Telugu play Kridabhiramam, is the present-day gummeta, and suggests that the name refers to the drum's deep, muffled (gumbhana) sound. [1]
construction: Accounts differ on the material. Mikkilineni describes the budige of the Jangam storytellers as made of bronze (kanchu) or brass, and notes that budiges are smaller than ordinary gummetas. On one side a cane hoop is fixed and covered with skin; the other side is left uncovered, like the mouth of a water jug (kuja). [1][2]

The Telugu Wikipedia article describes the gummeta as a clay vessel like a water jug whose bottom is removed and replaced with skin, the mouth end being left open, and English Wikipedia calls the gummetas of Burrakatha earthen drums. [8][3]

David Courtney describes the gummeta as a South Indian folk drum of which a smaller version is used in Andhra Pradesh for Burrakatha and a slightly larger one in Goa and Karnataka, and places it in the same class of instruments as the tumbak of Kashmir and the Middle Eastern darbuka, while noting that any historical link between them is unclear. [9]
playing: In Burrakatha the main storyteller (kathakudu) plays the tambura and keeps time with metal rings (andelu), while the two side-singers (vantalu) on either side play gummetas hung from the neck or shoulder so that the drum sits under the arm. [1][2][3][9]

The player strikes the skin with the fingers of the right hand and closes and opens the uncovered mouth with the other hand, producing a deep, muffled tone. Courtney notes that both hands are occasionally used on the skin. [2][8][9]

Mikkilineni gives the syllables of the side-singers' beat, such as 'daddotimi, tadimi tattaddhimi, takita tatadhimi', with ornamental 'tadiginatom' phrases and cries of 'arare' and 'bhali bhali' to spur the storyteller. He adds that a story can be told with just the three-stroke 'daddotimi', but skilled players use many classical rhythm patterns (varusalu) ending in cadences (muktayimpu), and in scenes of fury the paired gummetas sound like thunderbolts. 'Gummetas are the life of the story and of the storyteller,' he writes. [1]
Before a night performance, the Budige Jangams play the gummetas loudly at the main spots of the village while going around announcing where the story will be told and inviting everyone to come. [2]
cultural: The gummeta belongs to the Shaiva Jangam storytelling tradition. According to Mikkilineni, Jangams were already singing these stories by about 1150 CE, when Veerashaivism was spreading, and the Budaga (Beda) Jangams also conduct funeral rites for Dalit, Adivasi and other backward-class households, walking ahead of the bier to the cremation ground blowing a conch and ringing a bell. [1][2]

In older practice whole families performed together and the storyteller's wife sang the vanta. Among the Saradakandru of Telangana, who sing their Sarada katha to a shoulder-held tambura called sarada, a storyteller's two wives sing the vanta, while a storyteller with only one wife is accompanied by her playing the dakki, which they also call dimki. [1]

Mikkilineni names Burra Pantulu of Khammam, Doddarapu Venkataswamy, Tadikonda Subbayya and Yellamanda as masters of the gummeta; he and Machineni learnt many patterns from Yellamanda and used them to train the Burrakatha troupes of the Praja Natya Mandali. [1]
usage: Burrakatha is performed across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, and its three-person format of storyteller and two gummeta-playing side-singers carried over from the older Jangam katha into the modern Burrakathas on political and social themes, developed from the 1940s. Christians also used the form to spread their faith: Gera Premayya's Burrakatha 'Pandita Ramabai' includes a verse describing the art, with 'the pair of gummetas sounding tadhimi'. [1][3][10]

The drum is used in related storytelling traditions. In Rayalaseema the Pichhukuntla, who first used only a bell and a titti, took up the tambura and gummetas under Jangam influence, and Mikkilineni notes that the budiges used by Jangams in Telangana are of the same kind. The Telugu Wikipedia article adds that the gummeta is also used by Oggu Katha tellers and by some women who sing and beg with it alone. [11][8]

A related clay drum of the Gonds of Adilabad is called gumela. M. A. Rauf, quoted by Mikkilineni, describes it as a hollow cylindrical drum of potter's clay with goat skin stretched over one side, played during the Dandari dance, and a 2021 report lists the 'Ghumela' among the instruments that Gonds and Kolams play before the goddess Jangubai at Dandari-Gussadi. [12][13]

Mikkilineni lists the districts where Budige Jangams still lived by their traditional occupations in the early 1990s — Srikakulam, Visakhapatnam, East and West Godavari, Krishna, Guntur, Prakasam, Chittoor, Nellore, Nizamabad and Medak — and asked the government to extend to them the facilities given to other scheduled communities. [2]

uncertain: Material: Mikkilineni (1992) describes the Jangams' budige as brass or bronze, while Telugu Wikipedia and English Wikipedia describe the gummeta as earthen (clay). Both kinds may be in use.

English Wikipedia calls the gummetas 'earthen drums with two heads', but Mikkilineni, Telugu Wikipedia and David Courtney all describe one skin and an open end. Some present-day troupes may use a two-headed drum in the same role, which could explain the difference; this was not checked in a written source.

The name dakki is ambiguous: Brown's and Sankaranarayana's dictionaries define ḍakki as a small hourglass drum (damaru), and the Telangana Padakosam (2010) as a small dappu, whereas Mikkilineni uses dakki as a regional name for the budige or gummeta. It is not certain that the Saradakandru's dakki (dimki) is identical to the Burrakatha gummeta.
Sabdaratnakaram and G. N. Reddy's dictionaries give tudumu as a synonym of gummeta; see the Tudumu page.
The identification of the veeragumbhita in Kridabhiramam with the gummeta is a scholarly opinion reported by Mikkilineni (citing Tirumala Ramachandra), not a certainty.

summary: A single-headed 'string drum' whose skin is sounded through a gut string that the player pulls and plucks. Called jamidika by the Baindla priest-singers of Telangana and jamuku in north coastal Andhra, it accompanies the stories of Yellamma and other village goddesses.

about: The jamidika (జమిడిక) is the ritual instrument of the Baindlas, also called Bavanis, the hereditary priests and story-singers of the Madiga community in Telangana. [1][5][6] Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy writes that over time the Baindla jamidika came to be called jimilika and jamuku, and that anyone who has seen today's jamuku can picture the jamidika. [1] Jamuku is the name used in north coastal Andhra, where the instrument gives its name to Jamukula Katha and is also called jamilika or budiki. [2][7]

The Baindlas are known by the instrument. Bheemaiah quotes Sri Rama Raju's view that the Bavanis got their name from the bavanika they play, and notes that the bavanika is also called pamba; in Telangana Baindlas are also called Bavaneelavaru, Pambalavaru and Jamukulavaru. He calls the jamidika a cultural icon without which Baindla culture is unimaginable. [5][8]

The instrument has a long history. Mikkilineni quotes a verse from the Telugu work Kridabhiramam praising a Bavani singer who sang the stories of Parashurama before the goddess Ekavira with masterly playing, as evidence that Bavanis were already prominent in the Kakatiya period, and he writes that the javanika - 'today's jamuku' - accompanied their Yellamma stories with its 'jukajum, jukajum' sound. [1][2][4]
construction: The body is a hollow shell open at one end, described as shaped like a kuncham (a tapering grain measure) or as conical, and made of brass or wood; some are of bronze. [1][2][5] Sakshi describes the Baindla jamidika of Telangana as made of brass. [6] The closed end is covered with a thin skin: sources variously name the tender skin of a calf, a thin membrane-like buffalo skin, or frog skin. [5][2][7][9]

A small hole is made in the centre of the skin and a gut string - traditionally an animal sinew - is knotted and passed through it into the body. At the open end the string is tied to a short piece of wood or a small wooden roller, which may carry a bunch of small bells. [2][5][7] Newer jamukus are also made with rubber, wood, tin sheet, bronze or brass. [7][9]

According to the Sphoorthi Theatre account, early instruments were earthen pots covered with the belly skin of a dead ox, with the sinew of its spinal cord used as the string; wood and later copper, brass or bronze replaced the pot for durability. [10]
playing: The player holds the body against the side or under the arm, pulls the stick at the back to draw the string taut, and plucks or strums the string with the fingertips; tightening and loosening the pull changes the sound that comes from the skin. [2][5][6][9] The rhythm follows the tune of each song and is played forcefully at dramatic moments. [1][6]

In a Baindla performance the lead narrator sings in the middle while companions (vantas) beside him play jamidikas and sing the refrains. [1][6] In Mahabubnagar district two Baindla artists perform together, the narrator with a large jamidika and his partner with a smaller one tuned to a different note; in Nalgonda and Khammam districts the lead performer plays the jamidika while others add a small harmonium, cymbals and a small drum. [5] Baindlas play differently for weddings and for deaths. [1]

In Jamukula Katha of north coastal Andhra there are three performers - the narrator in the middle, one companion for humour and one for commentary - and the two companions play jamukus. In the budiki form of Srikakulam district, two budikis (jamukus) and the ankle bells are the only instruments, and the players hang the budikis from the armpit. [2]
cultural: The jamidika is believed to hold power. A myth recorded by Tangirala Venkata Subba Rao and cited by Bheemaiah says that when the goddess Renuka hid from her son Parashurama in a trough in the Madiga quarter, he came disguised as a Pambala playing the jamidika and prayed to her, and at its sound she came out; Baindlas hold a strong conviction about their instrument. [5]

Jamuku artists of north Andhra tell their own origin story: after killing the demon Suketu, the goddess Yellamma had the skin of his back stretched over a box, his spinal nerve made into the single string and the marrow of his leg into a small fitting, and so the jamuku was made. Villagers also believe that no evil wind, ghost or spirit can come as far as the jamuku's sound carries, and those who take up Jamukula Katha as a profession regard it as sacred. [7]

Baindlas serve as priests for the Madigas, conducting their weddings and mediating with village goddesses such as Yellamma, Maisamma and Pochamma; they believe that any lapse in this mediation can anger the goddesses and bring diseases such as plague and cholera on the village. [5][6] Mikkilineni adds that Baindlas perform only for Shaiva households, at weddings and at deaths. [1] Telugu Wikipedia notes that, because of untouchability, others would not touch the jamidike played by the Baindlas. [8]
Baindla children learn the jamidika, cymbals and harmonium by travelling with their parents and imitating them, and elders fear that children who study further will forget the family occupation. [5]
usage: In Telangana, Baindla artists play the jamidika while telling the stories of Renuka Yellamma, Pochamma, Maisamma and Poleramma at village goddess festivals. After bonalu offerings are made they stay at the shrine through the night, draw patterns (patnams) with turmeric and vermilion, and narrate the goddesses' histories until dawn in costumes such as Parashurama, Mandhata and Potharaju. [6] They also narrate the Yellamma story at local celebrations and Madiga weddings. [5]

In north coastal Andhra (Srikakulam, Vizianagaram and Visakhapatnam districts) and in the Godavari districts, Jamukula Katha - also called Bonela paata or Budiki paata - is performed by Mala and Madiga artists, with stories from the epics and local ballads. [2][7][9] In the 1940s the Praja Natya Mandali took up the form for social themes, and the poet-activist Subbarao Panigrahi of Sompeta composed many Jamukula Katha songs during the Srikakulam tribal peasant struggle. [7][11]

In Rayalaseema and Telangana the Asadulu, a priestly group among the Madigas, play their javanikas vigorously at village goddess festivals and sing the Yellamma story. [3] Mikkilineni also notes that Bavanis once told the Renuka (Yellamma) story over two nights while playing the javanika. [4]

The tradition is under strain. Sakshi reports that only a few Baindla story-singers remain in Telangana, finding work mainly in the Ashadha and Shravana months, and that the younger generation is not coming forward to learn; Bheemaiah describes the Baindla occupation as being on the verge of extinction. [6][5]

uncertain: Jemidike, jamidika and jamuku: the spelling 'Jemidike' was not found in any published source; it matches the Telugu form జమిడికె (jamidike) used on Telugu Wikipedia. Mikkilineni states that the Baindla jamidika came to be called jimilika and jamuku, so the three names are treated here as one instrument. Regional forms differ in material, size and song style: Mikkilineni notes that Baindla tunes differ a great deal from Jamukula Katha tunes. [1][8]

The name pamba is used for this instrument by Bheemaiah (citing Sri Rama Raju and the poet Arudra) and Telugu Wikipedia, but it is also the name of the pair of brass drums played by the Pambala community in Chittoor and coastal Andhra. The same word refers to different instruments in different regions. [5][8]

Classification: the jamidika is sometimes loosely called a friction drum, but every source consulted describes the string being plucked or strummed. English Wikipedia lists jamidika and jamuku among the names of the gubguba (ananda lahari) family and classes it as a composite chordophone; this page calls it a string drum. [12]

The skin is described differently: calf skin (Bheemaiah), a thin membrane-like buffalo skin ('gedela bakki charmam' - the exact meaning of bakki is unclear) (Mikkilineni), and frog skin (Telugu Wikipedia, Telugu Traditions). [5][2][7][9]
Sakshi calls Kridabhiramam a 13th-century work; its date was not checked for this page. [6]
In Srikakulam the jamuku-accompanied song is also called 'Budabukkala paata' from its 'budukku' sound (Mikkilineni). This is not the budabukka drum of the Budabukkala community. [2]

The Suketu myth and the belief that evil spirits keep away from the jamuku's sound come from Telugu Wikipedia sections not found in Mikkilineni's chapter; the Sphoorthi Theatre description of early clay-pot instruments is from a blog without references. [7][10]
Mikkilineni's chapter on the Asadulu says Madiga Asadulu play a 'chedika' as well as their javanikas; what the chedika is was not established. [3]

classification: Long curved horn (aerophone)
summary: A long, curved horn of the Gonds of Adilabad, played by Pardhan musicians. It sounds together with the tudum drum and the pepre shawm in the Dandari–Gussadi festival and at the Nagoba Jatara, and its call is likened to a conch summoning people to battle.

about: The kalikom is a long, curved horn used by the Gonds of the Adilabad region of northern Telangana. It is named among the instruments of the Dandari–Gussadi festival and of the Nagoba Jatara, the annual pilgrimage of the Mesram clan of Gonds [1][3][4][5].

A 2013 list of eighteen Gond instruments from Adilabad district records the kalikom, together with the sanai (shawm) and the kikiri fiddle, as an instrument of the Pardhans, the hereditary bards and musicians of the Gonds [6]. The kalikom was among the tribal and folk instruments shown at 'Adi Dhwani', a 2019 exhibition in Hyderabad of tribal and folk instruments, many of them collected by Professor Jayadheer Tirumala Rao [7].
construction: The English Wikipedia describes the kalikom as a long, curved horn made of brass or wood [1]. No detailed published account of its size, making or makers was found during this research [1].
playing: The kalikom is blown as a companion to drums. A Telugu description of the tudum drum says that when the tudum is played the kalikom is blown as an accompanying instrument [2].

Haimendorf's account of the Dandari season in the 1940s describes a visiting troupe arriving at night led by torch-bearers and musicians, among them 'a Pardhan trumpeting on a huge metal horn', and leaving again 'to the beating of dapna and kettle drums and the shrieking blasts from the Pardhan's large horn'. He did not give the horn a name [8].
cultural: The combined sound of the tudum and the kalikom is said to feel like hearing a conch that calls people to get ready for battle; the Adivasis describe it as the tudum pealing out and the kalikom crying out [2].

A 2013 list of Gond instruments names the kalikom among the instruments played by the Pardhans, and Haimendorf described the Pardhans as the hereditary bards who act as musicians at Gond rites, blowing their wind instruments at important moments [6][8].
usage: The kalikom is one of the instruments of the Dandari–Gussadi festival held around Diwali by the Raj Gonds and Kolams of Adilabad and neighbouring districts. Telugu and English accounts list it with the dappu, tudumu and pepre, and Village Square names it among the instruments used in Gussadi celebrations [1][3][5].

At the Nagoba Jatara at Keslapur in Indervelli mandal, the Deccan Chronicle reported in 2025 that the kalikom, dhol, thudum and pepri are played differently to suit each ritual or occasion, their sound resounding across Keslapur [4].

classification: Three-stringed bowed fiddle (chordophone) with a square, skin-covered wooden sound box
summary: A three-stringed bowed fiddle with a square, skin-covered wooden sound box, played by the Pardhan and Thoti bards of the Gonds in the Adilabad region. It accompanies Gond hymns and epics and clan-god rites, and is treated as sacred, personified as the ancestress Hirabai.

about: The kikri, also written kingri or khikri, is the fiddle of the Pardhans, the hereditary bards of the Raj Gonds of the Adilabad region in northern Telangana, and of the Thotis, a smaller community of Gond bards. The anthropologist Christoph von Fürer-Haimendorf, who studied the Adilabad Gonds in the 1940s, called the kingri 'the most important possession of a Pardhan' [1][2]. Telugu sources describe it as an instrument widely known in Gond society, on which Pardhans and Thotis sing the traditional stories of the Gond tribe [3][4].

The songs and stories of the Pardhans are the main store of Gond oral tradition. At the rites for each clan god (Persa Pen) the Pardhan attached to that god plays the fiddle and quietly sings the ancient hymns, and afterwards recites the myths of the origin of the Gonds and of the clan deities with two assistants [1].

Telugu writing compares the kikri with other folk fiddles of India, such as the ravanahatha of Rajasthan, and notes that although it was once found in several states where Gonds live, today it is used mainly by Gondi-speaking people in Telangana and Maharashtra [3].
construction: The kikri has a square wooden sound box covered with a skin membrane. A long bamboo neck runs through the box, and three tuning pegs are set at the other end of the bamboo [1][2][4]. The Hindu reported that the three strings and the hair of the bow are made of horse hair [2].

A Telugu description drawn from the book Mooladhwani says the resonator, about one and a half spans long, is made by hollowing out a piece of tree trunk and covering it with goat skin; a bamboo is pushed through it, and three holes at the other end hold tuning pegs called pootilu [3].

The bow is curved and hung with small bells (gajjelu) that jingle in time with the tune as it is drawn [2][3]. Haimendorf's drawing of a Pardhan's kingri shows a bow made of antelope horn, and he described the tiny bells on a bow of antelope horn and horse hair jingling softly as the musician played [1].

Instruments are kept for generations. In 2015 the Pardhan Mesram Tukdoji told The Hindu that his kingri was at least 200 years old and that its strings had not been replaced since he inherited it 52 years earlier [2].
playing: The kikri is played seated, held upright and bowed. Mesram Tukdoji explained that the instrument rests on the left shoulder while it is played [2]. The Telugu description says the player presses the box with his chin and draws the bow across the strings much as a violin is played [3].

Haimendorf recorded how the Pardhan Chitru performed the Gond creation epic after a Persa Pen feast. After tuning his three-stringed fiddle he played a short prelude, then sang, with his son and nephew joining in at the end of each verse while the son kept rhythm on a small pair of cymbals. Sung verses alternated with spoken declamation and short passages on the fiddle, and during the chorus he played louder and more vigorously than when accompanying his own solo [1].

At festivals it is usually the most prominent Pardhan who plays the kingri, while younger men blow trumpets and beat drums [1][4]. According to the Telugu account, the kikri is played together with a pair of shawms called pepre and a skin drum called dakki [3].
cultural: The kikri is regarded as sacred. In a Gond origin myth recorded by Haimendorf, when the fire goddess threatened Pahandi Kupar Lingal and the Gonds, Hirabai, the mother of the young Hira who was sent to help them, turned herself into a kingri so that she could rest on her son's shoulder as his guardian. As his bow moved 'ki-ki-ki' over the strings, the goddess was spellbound and the rites could continue. In another version the danger came from the untamed clan god Persa Pen, and Haimendorf wrote that most Gonds believed the Pardhan's playing on the kingri during Persa Pen rites was necessary to tame the fierce god and protect the worshippers [1].

Present-day accounts keep this identity. Telugu sources call the instrument Hirabai kikri and associate it with Hira Sukka, regarded as the religious and musical teacher of the Pardhans and the Gonds [3]. Mesram Tukdoji told The Hindu that the kingri is female and is called Hirabai, and that when it is not in use it is tied to its male counterpart, Heerasukka, which is shaped like a small sword [2].

Customs surround its handling. According to Tukdoji, the kingri may be played only by married men [2]. At a Persa Pen feast Haimendorf saw the Pardhan Chitru sacrifice a small chicken in front of his fiddle, which, according to myth, is the transformed body of his ancestress Hirabai; and in a Gond legend he recorded, the wise Pardhan Hirasuka first washes the 'leg' of his fiddle Hirabai before washing his own feet [1].
The Hindu also reported a belief that gods who were angry with the tribe could be pacified only when Pardhan elders played the 'Dunadi vaja', the sacred stringed instrument [2].
usage: The kikri is played during Persa Pen clan-god rites and other religious ceremonies, and at rites connected with births, marriages and deaths among the Gonds [1][2][5]. A list of Gond instruments compiled in Adilabad notes that the kikri is played during worship of the gods and at the time of death [6].

It is prominent at the Nagoba Jatara of the Mesram clan of Gonds at Keslapur in Indervelli mandal, Adilabad district, where The Hindu photographed the Pardhan Mesram Tukdoji playing the kingri at the Nagoba temple and described the chorus that he and his team sing to its accompaniment during the jatara [2].

The Thotis, like the Pardhans, sing Gond history at annual jataras, recite stories and folk songs, and perform with the kingri at marriages and funerals; Haimendorf noted that stories of the god Bhimana are their special repertoire [1][5].

Haimendorf observed in the 1940s that where Pardhans gave up their fiddle and their old association with the Gonds, cultural life suffered [1]. A 2025 study of the Thoti community found that the playing of the kikri and related instruments by Thoti men at festivals and funerals in Gond homes has greatly declined, although the community still plays the kikri [5]. The instrument has been shown in exhibitions of tribal instruments in Hyderabad, including Adya Kala's 'Adi Dhwani' [7].
