classification: Veena-like plucked string instrument with a bamboo neck and dried-gourd resonators (chordophone)
summary: A veena-like string instrument with a bamboo neck and dried bottle-gourd resonators, played by Dakkali bards (and once by the Chenchus of the Nallamala forests) to accompany ballads of Telangana's folk heroes. Its best-known player, Darshanam Mogilaiah, plays a 12-fret version and received the Padma Shri in 2022.

about: The kinnera (కిన్నెర) is a stringed instrument native to nomadic communities of the Deccan plateau such as the Dakkali and the Chenchu. A kinnera performance combines singing and playing, and its ballads are sung mainly in rustic Telugu [1]. The scholar Jayadhir Tirumala Rao traces its origins to around the 4th century CE in the Deccan, and says the Dakkali of the Mahabubnagar region, near the Nallamala forest, have performed with it since at least the 12th century [1].

Much like the Saraswati veena, it is made from natural materials: a bamboo neck with resonators of sun-dried, hollowed bottle gourds. Kinneras are made with seven, nine, 12 or 13 frets; larger instruments have three gourd resonators and smaller ones two [1][3]. It has also been described as a folk veena that wandering bards used to narrate community histories and folklore [11].

The best-known player today is Darshanam Mogilaiah (also spelled Mogulaiah) of Nagarkurnool district, whose kinnera has 12 frets, or steps (mettu). He received the Padma Shri in 2022, cited as the last player to have mastered the 12 steps of the instrument [8][4].
construction: Accounts of the traditional instrument describe a bamboo neck, dried and hollowed gourds as resonators, strings of human hair or animal nerve, and frets made of pangolin scales fixed in place with honey-wax (beeswax) [3][2]. The strings were also once made of women's hair and horse-tail hair, but these have long been replaced by thin metal strings [1].

The right gourd is essential. According to Jayadhir Tirumala Rao, the Chenchus lost the instrument about half a century ago when the gourd used for its resonator became extinct in their region, and shrinking forests have made suitable gourds and pangolins hard to obtain. Making the kinnera, like playing it, requires special skills [3][1].

Mogilaiah's family has made its own kinneras for generations [5]. His two-stringed instrument is described as made from bamboo, the dried outer shell of round bottle gourds, honeycomb, wax, bull horn, beads, mirrors and peacock feathers, and its strings of goat nerve have been replaced with metal ones [4][8]. In 2014 the researcher Dasari Ranga explained that Mogilaiah fixes pieces of dried fruit, coconut or dried horn at 12 places on the instrument so that its two strings give different tunes [6].

Mogilaiah's forefathers made kinneras with seven steps and his father made one with nine. The elders told him a kinnera could not have more than eleven steps, but over time he built one with twelve [5]. His instrument is elaborately painted and decorated, and carries a small wooden turtle puppet that bows, jumps and salutes the audience [2].

A 1992 survey of Telugu folk arts describes a simpler tribal kinnera: a hollow bamboo about 20 inches long with four frets fixed to its middle with wax, two strings stretched over the frets, and a resonator at one end of the bamboo [9].
playing: The kinnera player accompanies his or her own singing. The ballads are interspersed with short, often dramatic spoken passages, and the performer's tone of voice, facial expressions and body language change with the mood of the song [1].

Describing Dakkali Balamma in her eighties, Scroll wrote that her kinnera produced a melodious, sharp sound as she strummed it, and that her grasp of shruti (pitch) and laya (rhythm) remained firm [1]. Mogilaiah is known for making up songs within minutes on subjects ranging from people to nature [5].
cultural: The Dakkali are a Dalit sub-caste of troubadours described as dependents of the Madigas. Historically one section of the Dakkali sang the Jambava (Jamba) Puranam, which explained their subservience to their chief patrons the Madigas, while another section played the kinnera. Both lived on alms from the Madigas, who rewarded performers with money, food and clothes [2][1][5].

A story told among the tribes explains why the Chenchus gave up the instrument: a woman cutting vegetables was so lost in the music of her husband's kinnera that she cut up her infant as well, and the horrified tribe banned the instrument from the hills [2][1].
According to Jayadhir Tirumala Rao, when the Dakkali community inherited the kinnera it reduced the number of frets to seven, purportedly in honour of the Chenchus [3].

The art is passed down within families. Mogilaiah is the fifth generation of kinnera players in his family and learned from his father Yellaiah, travelling with him from the age of eight. Balamma learned from her father and remembered travelling from village to village on donkeys to play and sing [5][4][2].

Mogilaiah has described the instrument's place in village life: his family did not beg while playing but performed wherever they were asked, sang through the night in a house where someone had died to console the bereaved, and sang for people bitten by snakes, saying that along with medicine the songs helped cure them [4]. He also says the kinnera has no caste: besides the Dakkali and Chenchu, he has seen a man of the Tenugu caste practise it, knew Muslim families who performed it, and has heard that even Nawabs made and played it [5].

The name kinnera also appears in older Telugu literature. According to the 1992 survey, Krishnadevaraya's 16th-century poem Amuktamalyada lists a 'buruma kinnera' among the instruments of its day, and describes Dasari singers of the Vijayanagara period, who served as gurus and priests to the Mala and Madiga communities, singing songs to a kinnera called 'bandalika' as they went about seeking alms [13].
usage: Kinnera ballads celebrate local heroes remembered for helping the poor, such as Pandugolla (Panduga) Sayanna, an 18th-century figure, Miya Saab (Meera Saab), Endavetla Fakeeraiah, Bandolla Kurumanna and Vettem Ranganayakamma, as well as stories of royal families [2][4][5][7]. Songs from the Jamba Puranam are also sung with the kinnera [1][11].

The tradition is centred on the old Mahabubnagar region of southern Telangana. The last performers are reported in Mahabubnagar and Vikarabad districts, with possibly a few more in Karnataka, Adilabad district and the Gond areas of Madhya Pradesh [1]. A 1992 account also records that Gondhali storytellers of the Aare community in Telangana are said to have once told their stories with a maddela drum and a kinnera, though no such troupes remained [10].

In August 2015 a team from the Telangana Rachayithala Vedika and the University of Hyderabad, including Jayadhir Tirumala Rao and G. Manoja of Palamuru University, took the Dakkali performer Pochayya and his kinnera to Appapur in the Nallamala forests on the International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples. Elderly Chenchus recognised the instrument, and a few played it from memory after nearly fifty years [1][3].
Mogilaiah reached a wide audience when he sang the title song of the Telugu film Bheemla Nayak (2022), which draws on the Miya Saab folklore he had sung for decades [4].

The kinnera is close to extinction. In 2019 Scroll estimated that only about a dozen people in India still played it, and Dakkali Balamma, the only known woman performer, died in December 2018 [1][2]. Mogilaiah has received the Telangana government's Ugadi Puraskaram (2015), a monthly pension and a lesson in the Class 8 textbook, but an effort to teach the kinnera at Potti Sreeramulu Telugu University found few takers [1][2][5]. A 2021 review of the study Mula Dhwani notes that only one person can still play the 12-step kinnera [12].

uncertain: Community of Darshanam Mogilaiah: The News Minute, The Indian Express and the Ministry of Tribal Affairs describe him as from a Madiga (Dalit) family; Scroll calls him part of the Dakkali tribe (the Dakkali are described as a Madiga sub-caste).

Spellings vary between sources: Mogilaiah/Mogulaiah (Telugu మొగిలయ్య/మొగులయ్య); Pochayya/Pochaiah; Pandugolla/Panduga/Pandaga Sayanna; Endavetla/Endematla/Endamatla Fakeeraiah; Miya Saab/Meera Saab/Mir Saab (Sakshi: మీర్‌సాబ్); Bandolla Kurumanna/Kurmanna.

Number of strings: The Indian Express and the Ministry of Tribal Affairs call Mogilaiah's kinnera two-stringed, while the 1992 Mikkilineni survey and The Hans India call the kinnera multi-stringed (and the same survey then describes a two-string, four-fret tribal kinnera without naming the tribe).

Fret materials on Mogilaiah's 12-step kinnera are not clearly documented: pangolin scales are described for older instruments, while sources list bull horn among his materials and Dasari Ranga (Times of India, 2014) mentions dried fruit, coconut or horn fixed at 12 places.
'Honey-wax' / 'honey wax' / Telugu 'మైనం' in the sources has been rendered as beeswax.
The 4th-century origin and 12th-century Dakkali dates are claims by Jayadhir Tirumala Rao as quoted by Scroll; they were not independently confirmed.

Fret counts: The Hindu (2015) says the Dakkali reduced the frets to seven in honour of the Chenchus; The News Minute says Mogilaiah's forefathers used seven and his father nine; The Hindu (2017) describes a 13-fret Chenchu instrument in Haimendorf's photograph; at the 2015 Appapur visit a blind Chenchu man said he was used to a 12-fret version (Scroll).
Dakkali Balamma's age: The Hindu (August 2017) says she was 95, while Scroll (2019) says she was 86 about four years earlier.
The Gondhali (Aare) use of a kinnera is reported as hearsay ('it is said') in the 1992 survey.

The kinnera named in Amuktamalyada ('buruma kinnera', 'bandalika') is known here only through the 1992 survey's summary; whether it was the same instrument as the Dakkali and Chenchu kinnera is not established.
None of the sources consulted gives a date of death for Mogilaiah; the Ministry of Tribal Affairs page is written in the past tense, so his current status was not assumed either way.

classification: Concussion idiophone: pairs of short, shaped wooden sticks struck together, sometimes fitted with bells and jingling rings
communities: Village Kolatam troupes of men, women and children
summary: Kolatam karralu are the short, polished wooden sticks that dancers strike together, against their own and their partners' sticks, in the Kolatam stick dance. Traditional sticks are shaped from hard timber, taper at both ends and may carry small bells and jingling rings.

about: Kolatam (kola, 'stick', and ata, 'play' or 'dance') is a group song-dance in which performers strike short sticks together in rhythm while moving in circles [1][2]. C. P. Brown's dictionary (1903) defines kolatamu as a dance in a ring in which sticks are struck together in harmony, and notes that a single stick is also called by this name [3]. The sticks, called kolalu or kolatam karralu, are both the dancers' prop and the main percussion instrument of the dance [1][4].

Kolatam has a long recorded history. Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy notes that Palkuriki Somanatha refers to 'kolata godiya' in his Panditaradhya Charitra, and that sculptures of women dancing Kolatam can still be seen on the walls of the Vijayanagara ruins and on the enclosure walls of the Srisailam temple [1].
construction: Mikkilineni, drawing on the research of folklorist Bittu Venkateswarlu, describes Kolatam sticks as thin at the start, swelling in the middle and thin again at the end, with a grip for holding. The sticks are chosen from strong, heartwood-rich (cheva) timbers such as billudu, chandra, epe, rela, teak and egisa, and are carefully finished [1]. In Brown's dictionary cheva means the heart or core of a tree [5], chandra is an acacia [6] and rela is the Indian laburnum, Cassia fistula [7].

Jingles are added for sound: andelu (jingling rings) are fixed near the grip and gajjelu (small bells) at the end of each stick, which gives a sweet sound while playing [1]. The sticks are brightly coloured; each player is described carrying colourful kola sticks [1], and a 2014 Deccan Chronicle report from Adilabad describes 'special decorated sticks, kolalu' used just as in Dandiya [4].
playing: Players first stand in a circle and pray to their chosen deity. They then stand in pairs facing each other and strike the sticks rhythmically; when the leader calls out a rhythmic phrase to raise the speed, the circle divides into inner and outer rings. Each pair (uddi) strikes sticks with each other, and the leader sets the rhythm with syllables that vary from region to region, such as 'taka taka tayyaku diddimi' or 'kolu kolu kolanna' [1].

Each song with its movement pattern is called a kopu. A kopu starts with the song and dance together (ettugada), shifts from the second to the third speed in an energetic section called usettu, where the players leap and sing, and is brought to a stop by the leader's closing phrase (muktayimpu) [1]. The troupe usually has twenty to forty players, always in even numbers, led by a leader known as Kolanna pantulu, pennuddi or ayyavaru, and all the players tie gajjelu to their ankles [1].

In jada kopu (braid) Kolatam, an even number of ropes is tied to a high branch, often of a tamarind tree, and each dancer holds one rope; moving in and out in two groups, they weave the ropes into a braid while singing and then unweave it by dancing in reverse. A single wrong step tangles the braid, which makes this the most demanding form of Kolatam [1][2]. A similar rope form, pinnal kolattam, is known in Tamil Nadu [8].
cultural: Kolatam is devotional as well as recreational. In villages it is played at night during leisure time; troupes carry a pole of the deity from house to house and perform before each home, and they also perform at big fairs, temple festivals and in the streets [1]. Telugu Wikipedia notes performances at the jataras of village goddesses such as Uradamma, Gandi Maisamma, Gangadevi, Katta Maisamma, Pothalingamma and Poleramma [2].

Discipline is part of the tradition. The leader decides the place and time of performance, the players follow the guru's word, and the leader is expected to be healthy and expert in rhythm, tala, songs and play; in some areas the leader carries a whip on his shoulder and cracks it to warn those who break discipline [1]. During the fast sections, coloured powder, flowers, sandal paste and rose water are sprinkled over the dancers to spur them on [1].

Kolatam also has a place in festivals and schooling. In Telangana it is performed during Holi and during Bathukamma Navaratri, when it is compared with the Dandiya of Durga Navaratri [4]. Mikkilineni recalls that girls' jada kopu Kolatam was once taught as an exercise in evening drill classes, and that Telangana Kolatam songs include dialogues depicting quarrels between husband and wife [1].
usage: Kolatam is performed across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Names of kopus vary by region; in the Palnadu area they include the prarthana (prayer), uddi tirugudu, Krishna, Kamsa, jada, Bharata, bhama, lali and lanke kopus [1].

In Adilabad district, Kolatam artists from Deepaidguda village in Jainad mandal performed at the collectorate in 2014, and Jada Koppula Aata, a related traditional dance, was reported to be popular in only a few villages in the eastern part of the district [4]. Kolatam songs there are sung by elders to harmonium and talalu, while in the traditional form described by Mikkilineni musicians in the centre of the circle play maddela, harmonium and tappeta [4][1].

classification: Drum (membranophone) of the mridangam type, used to accompany singing
summary: The Telugu name for a mridangam-type skin drum that accompanies song in folk theatre: Tholu Bommalata shadow puppetry, Chindu Bhagavatam, Yakshaganam and street-theatre troupes, daytime impersonators, kolatam and bhajans, usually together with harmonium and cymbals.

about: Maddela (మద్దెల) is the Telugu form of the Sanskrit word mardala. Telugu dictionaries define it as a skin drum played to accompany singing and list mridangamu, murajamu and mardalamu among its synonyms; C. P. Brown's dictionary (1903) derives it from Sanskrit mṛdaṅga and glosses it 'a small drum', and Nalimela Bhaskar's Telangana Padakosam (2010) glosses it simply as mridangam. [1][2]

The word is old in Telugu literature. Vavilla's dictionary (1949) quotes the Ranganatha Ramayanam, where the maddela sounds 'dimi dimi' as actresses dance to songs, and Srinatha's Palnati Veera Charitra describes a court dancer who ties on her ankle bells and takes her place 'between the maddela and the cymbals' before she begins to dance. [1][3]

Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy points to older evidence as well: sculptures in a temple at the eastern end of the Ramappa tank bund at Palampet, from the Kakatiya period, showing women playing the maddela while dancers perform, and a verse of Hala's Prakrit anthology Gatha Saptashati (3.53), which in the Telugu rendering he quotes says that the maddela sounds sweet only as long as there is food (rice) on its face and grumbles harshly without it. [4][5]
construction: The sources consulted give little detail on how folk maddelas are made. Dictionaries classify the maddela as a charma vadyam (an instrument sounded on a stretched skin) and equate it with the mridangam, and the Gatha Saptashati verse quoted by Mikkilineni refers to food applied to the drum's face to give it a sweet tone. [1][5]

The maddela is also used as a yardstick in descriptions of tribal drums: M. A. Rauf, quoted by Mikkilineni, describes the Savara daggudu as shaped like a maddela, and the para of the Raj Gonds as like a maddela but two feet long, with goat skin on both ends played with the fingers. [6]
playing: The maddela is an accompanying drum, normally heard with a harmonium for the drone (sruti) and cymbals (talalu). In Tholu Bommalata, the singers, the harmonium player, the cymbal player, the maddela player and the person making sound effects all sit behind the screen, and the instrumentalists also sing the chorus (vanta); the players also stamp on wooden boards under their feet in battle scenes and when chariots or horses run. [7]

A 2025 research paper in the Telugu journal Auchithyam likewise names maddelu, harmonium and cymbals as the instruments of traditional puppet troupes, the Telugu Wikipedia article on Tholu Bommalata lists harmonium, cymbals, tokkudu billa (foot clappers), maddela, dappu and ankle bells, and the MAP Academy's encyclopedia lists the 'muddalam and mridangam' among Tholu Bommalata's percussion, with cymbals, harmonium, mukhaveena and conch. [8][9][10]

In Chindu Bhagavatam of Telangana, the Chindu Bhagavatulu dance their steps to maddelu, cymbals, ankle bells, harmonium, a gourd pipe (poongi) and sannayi, according to a 2024 article by Osmania University researcher Bashipangu Venkanna. Mikkilineni lists mridangam, cymbals, ankle bells and harmonium as the main instruments of the Chindu women's performances, with the actors singing the chorus from the background and women playing the cymbals. [11][12]

Skill on the drum was valued: Mikkilineni notes that the celebrated pagati veshagadu (daytime impersonator) Bhagavatula Kumaraswamy, who could play thirty-two different roles, was famous for his maddela playing and could reproduce the maddela wonderfully with his mouth. [13]
cultural: Because it accompanies devotional theatre, the maddela is part of ritual as well as entertainment. A Tholu Bommalata show opens with a mangala harati sung in raga Todi and a prayer to Vighneswara so that no obstacles arise, and a Chindu Bhagotam begins with prayers to Ganapati and Saraswati. [7][11]

Mikkilineni records that the Chindu performers play an 'Ellamma ata' in every village where they perform, praying that the village stay green and prosperous, and that people in many villages of Nizamabad district still believed this performance keeps famine away. [12]
usage: Mikkilineni's survey shows the maddela across Telugu folk theatre. The Yanadi Bhagavatam troupes of coastal Andhra, which staged Usha Parinayam, Krishna leelalu, Savitri and Sasirekha Parinayam through the night, used the maddela, cymbals and a harmonium. In Rayalaseema, troupes staging mythological plays in the village bazaar would first make a festive noise with maddela and cymbals. [14][15]

In Telangana, the Gondhali performers who play street bhagotams in villages of the Are community use harmonium and maddela as accompaniment, and in earlier Gondhali Burrakathas one man played the maddela, another the kinnera and a third the cymbals. The Gante Bhagavatulu (Telaga Dasaris) sing their kirtanas to a harmonium drone with maddela and cymbals. [16][17]

The Kuchipudi Bhagavatulu's daytime impersonations (pagati veshalu), such as the Ardhanarishvara vesham, were accompanied by at least two Bhagavatulu playing harmonium and maddela, and kolatam groups and Pandari bhajana singers also use the maddela with harmonium, cymbals and other instruments. [18][19][20]
Bashipangu Venkanna writes that Chindu Bhagotam is disappearing in Telangana for lack of training and calls for a government academy for the art. [11]

uncertain: No source consulted describes how a folk maddela is built (wood, skins, lacing or tuning), so the construction section stays brief. Dictionaries equate maddela with mridangam, and Mikkilineni sometimes writes 'mridangam' for the same folk-theatre drum (for example for the Chindu performers), so the two names may be used interchangeably in practice.
The MAP Academy text lists 'muddalam and mridangam' as two percussion instruments of Tholu Bommalata; 'muddalam' is probably another spelling of maddela, but this is not confirmed.
The Gatha Saptashati verse is known here only through Mikkilineni's Telugu rendering (credited to P. S. R. Appa Rao); the Prakrit original may name a different drum (for example muraja).
Brown's dictionary calls the maddela 'a small drum', while descriptions of related instruments suggest a double-headed drum; the size is not documented in the sources read.

classification: Small double-headed hourglass hand drum (membranophone), of the damaru type
summary: A small double-headed hourglass drum - the Telangana name for the damaru held by Shiva - which gives the Oggu Katha ballad tradition of the Kuruma and Golla communities its name. It is sounded at the start of the story and in many scenes of the narration.

about: Oggu (ఒగ్గు) is the name a section of the Shaiva tradition in Telangana gives to the damaru, the small hourglass drum held by Shiva; it is also called jeggu or jaggu. [1][3] Telugu Wikipedia describes oggu as a purely native word heard only in the Telangana region. [3] Because storytellers use this drum while narrating, their art is called Oggu Katha, 'the story told with the oggu'. [1][4][7]

The oggu belongs to the Kurumas and Gollas (Yadavas), pastoral communities whose caste deities Mallanna (Mallikarjuna) and Beerappa are the heroes of the stories. [1][5] The Kurumas who tell these stories are also called oggollu or baggu vallu, and they serve as priests within their own community. [1]
construction: Sources describe the oggu as a skin-headed drum resembling the damaru in Shiva's hand. [6][9] According to Telugu Wikipedia it is about a hand-span (janedu) long, with a middle section of brass or wood and goat skin stretched tight over both ends. [3]
playing: Before a story begins, the performers play the dolu, sound a veeranam and rattle the damaru ('dada dada'), and their first prayer is to the goddess Ganga. [1] During the narration the oggu is played in many scenes to keep time and mark events, and it can be treated as a character in the story - for example, it is cradled like a baby when a lullaby scene comes. In the flow of the story it is a little less prominent than the big dolu drum. [3]

An Oggu Katha troupe usually has five to ten members: a lead narrator and an assistant in front, and behind them the players of the dolu, the talam (cymbals) and the kanjira, all of whom also sing the refrains. [1] V6 Velugu lists a large dolu, cymbals and the oggu as the main instruments of the form. [6]

A 2025 study notes a difference in instruments between performers: priests who serve at the big Mallanna temples such as Ainavolu, Komuravelli, Odela and Srisailam use the jaggu, an instrument like Shiva's damarukam, and are therefore called jaggulu, while other performers use the oggu dolu and cymbals. [5]
Mikkilineni also records Yadava storytellers in Telangana who dress as women, tie on ankle bells and dance with an oggu in hand, accompanied by a large dolu, big cymbals and chorus singers. [2]
cultural: According to the veteran performer Chukka Sattaiah, as recorded by Mikkilineni, the name has this origin: Veerabhadra and Mallikarjuna carried the damaru, called jaggu, and two hundred years ago Sattaiah's forefathers, grazing the sheep that Mallikarjuna had given them, told these stories under the trees in the forest to the sound of the jaggu. Over time the 'baggu katha told with the jaggu' came to be called oggu katha. [1]

For the Kurumas, Oggu Katha is a religious duty as well as an art. The Mallanna story is told at Kuruma weddings, and the marriage is performed only after it has been told. Each priest-storyteller once had fixed village and taluk boundaries: he could not conduct weddings in another's area or tell the stories at other times, on pain of expulsion from the caste. Chukka Sattaiah himself is said to have been expelled before he turned Oggu Katha into a popular stage art that the caste gurus later followed. [1] A copper-plate record concerning Birla Buchhaiah of Atmakur (Nalgonda district) documents the hereditary (mirasi) rights of the Oggus to perform Beerappa festivals. [5]

Telugu Wikipedia describes an initiation called oggu diksha. With the permission of caste elders, a trainee goes to a Shaiva shrine, spreads a mat in the temple courtyard, wears sacred ash and meditates on Mallanna; senior oggus then teach him a mantra and bless him, and he wears a necklace of seven cowrie shells said to be given by Yellamma. Only after this is he entitled to tell the stories of Beeranna and Mallanna. [3] English Wikipedia links the seven shells to a legend in which Mallanna turned the seven brothers of his bride into dogs and, when she pleaded for them, allowed them to become oggus who narrate his story. [4][5]
Oggu Katha opens with praise of the goddess Ujjaini Mahankali, followed by prayers to Ganapati and Sarada; V6 Velugu notes this as unusual, since most Hindu performances begin with Ganapati. [1][6]
usage: The oggu is used in Oggu Katha, the sung, danced and acted narration of the lives of Mallanna, Beerappa, Yellamma, Nalla Pochamma, Mandhata and other figures. [4][5][6] Performances take place at Kuruma and Golla weddings, at Beerappa festivals and at Mallanna temples and jataras. [1][4][5]

The form belongs to Telangana. In 1992 Mikkilineni found it mainly in Warangal, Nalgonda and Hyderabad districts, with about fifty troupes; later reports add Karimnagar and Rangareddy, and V6 Velugu notes that the Vemulawada area has many troupes. [1][8][6]

Well-known Oggu Katha artists include Chukka Sattaiah of Janagama, who received a Sangeet Natak Akademi award and an honorary doctorate from Potti Sreeramulu Telugu University, and Midde Ramulu of Karimnagar district; Jamma Mallari is known as the first woman to perform Oggu Katha. [8][4][5] In 2022 The Hans India reported that about 300 artistes depended on the art and that a troupe earned around Rs 5,000 per performance, with only a couple of bookings a month. [8]

uncertain: The word oggu is used loosely: it names the small hourglass drum, but the big barrel drum of the same tradition is called oggu dolu (also Veerappa dolu), and English sources often mix up the Oggu Katha instruments (English Wikipedia names a big drum 'rana bheri' and a horn 'napheera'). This page covers only the small hourglass drum. [1][4]

The physical description (hand-span long, brass or wooden middle, goat skin on both sides) comes only from a section of Telugu Wikipedia without an inline citation and was not confirmed elsewhere. No source describes whether the oggu has knotted striker cords like a typical damaru, how its heads are fixed, or who makes it; Mikkilineni's phrase 'rattling the damaru' suggests it is shaken. [3][1]

C. P. Brown's dictionary (1903) gives oggu only as a verb ('to yield, to bend, to spread') with no drum meaning, which fits Telugu Wikipedia's statement that the drum sense is a regional Telangana word. [10][3]

The oggu diksha and the seven-shell legend are taken from Wikipedia articles without inline citations; the seven brothers turned into dogs also appear in Sarma (2025), but the link to the shell necklace was not confirmed. [3][4][5]
Sarma (2025) cites N. Jnaneswara Bhikshu's PhD thesis (Shodhganga) for the jaggu/jaggulu distinction; the thesis itself could not be opened. [5]

In Rayalaseema (Kurnool district) the Goravayyas also play a damaru in Mallanna worship, and Telugu Wikipedia says some there are called oggappalu because of a ritual called oggu seva. Whether this is connected with the Telangana oggu was not established.

Mikkilineni's chapter gives two different openings: in one place the performers first pray to Ganga after sounding the dolu and damaru, in another the story opens with praise of Ujjaini Mahankali. Practice may differ between troupes. [1][6]

Mikkilineni reports that Chukka Sattaiah's storytelling group called its stories 'Veerappa katha', about Veerabhadra, whereas other sources treat Beerappa as a separate Kuruma deity; the relation between the names was not resolved. [1][5]

classification: Paired drums (membranophone) with brass bodies, beaten with two sticks
summary: A pair of brass drums beaten with two sticks by the Pambala community, from whom the drum takes its name. It leads village-goddess processions and accompanies the night-long Ankamma stories of the Pambalas; it is used only for worship and ritual, never for concerts.

about: The pamba (పంబ) is the drum from which the Pambala community takes its name. C. P. Brown's Telugu-English Dictionary (1903) defines pamba as 'a kind of drum' and the Pambalavandlu as those who play the pamba. [6] Edgar Thurston's Castes and Tribes of Southern India (1909) describes the Pambalas as 'drum (pamba) people', a section of the Malas who act as musicians at Mala weddings and at festivals in honour of their deities. [1]

The drum is usually spoken of as a pair - pamba joda, 'a pair of pambas'. [3][5] Pamba Katha, the goddess ballads of the Pambalas, is one of the Telugu story-singing forms named after its accompanying instrument, alongside Jamukula Katha, Burra Katha and Oggu Katha. [4] Thurston also records a similar name, Pambaikkaran, as an occupational name for Paraiyans who play a drum called pambai. [2]
construction: According to Telugu Wikipedia, pambas always come as a pair and must be made of brass, and two sticks are needed to play them. [5]
playing: The pambas are beaten with two sticks. Their sound is described as not sweet but stirring - meant to rouse heroic fervour rather than to please as music - and the instrument is never used in concerts, only at times of worship and ritual. [5]

In a Pambala performance of the Ankamma story, the companions (vantas) play the pamba pair and blow the titti (a bellows drone) to give the drone pitch, while the narrator, dressed as a prince, dances vigorously with a large sword in his right hand and a small blade called amajala in his left. This description is by Dr. Tangirala Venkata Subba Rao, quoted by Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy. [3][5]
cultural: The Pambalas are priests to the Malas and have conducted their funeral rites, including the pedda karma. [5] Thurston records them reciting the story of Ankamma and making muggu (floor designs) at the peddadinamu death ceremony of the Gamallas. [1] The goddess worshipped in their tradition is called Marasapu (or Murasapu) Ankamma. [3][5]

When rains failed or disease struck a village, Pambalas were called to play their drums and tell stories through the night at the rites (kolupulu) held to appease the village goddesses, and it was said that jataras could not be completed without their instruments. [5]

In Chittoor district, when a family sets out for a village-goddess puja, the Pambalas must walk ahead of them playing the pambas all the way from the house to the temple. The sound rouses such fervour that some devotees go into trance (punakam). [5]
usage: The pamba accompanies Pamba (Pambala) Katha - above all the Ankamma katha sung in the coastal 'Sarkar' districts of Andhra - as well as processions of festival idols, jataras and village-goddess worship. [3][5]

In 1992 Mikkilineni wrote that Pambala story performances, once common at goddess festivals in coastal Andhra, were still held wherever village goddesses are worshipped but were gradually disappearing. [3] Telugu Wikipedia reports that the instrument is still widely used in village-goddess pujas in Chittoor district. [5]

The name also appears in Telangana, but with a different meaning: Bheemaiah notes that the Baindlas there are also called Pambalavaru and quotes the poet Arudra that Bavanis are called Pambalas because of an instrument called pamba - which in those accounts is another name for the jamidika string drum rather than the pair of brass drums. [7][8]

traditions: Village goddess processions, kolupulu and jataras

uncertain: Most physical details come from Telugu Wikipedia (a pair, brass, two sticks). The book it cites (Mikkilineni, 1992) does not contain these details, and no other written source describing the pamba's shape, heads or makers was found. [5][3]

Telugu Wikipedia illustrates the article with photographs from Chittoor district whose captions call the instrument pommalu or pommala jodu; whether pommalu is simply a local pronunciation of pambalu was not confirmed. [5]

The word pamba names different instruments in different places: the pair of brass drums of the Pambalas of Chittoor and coastal Andhra, and, according to Bheemaiah (citing Sri Rama Raju and Arudra) and Telugu Wikipedia, the jamidika string drum of the Baindlas in Telangana. Which instrument today's 'Pambala' Ankamma performers in Telangana use was not established from written sources. [7][8]

The community is described differently: Thurston calls the Pambalas a section of the Malas; Tangirala Venkata Subba Rao (via Mikkilineni) calls them Harijans 'of Ayyagari darsanam'; Telugu Wikipedia lists Pambala as the 21st caste in group A of Andhra Pradesh's Backward Classes list; and Brown's 1903 dictionary describes Pambalavandlu as wandering fortune-tellers. These classifications were not checked against official lists. [1][3][5][6]
Thurston lists the Tamil pambai (played by Paraiyans) next to the Telugu Pambalas, but no source consulted states that the two drums are the same instrument. [2]
Telugu Wikipedia's section on the community's history (rain and disease rites, funeral duties) is uncited. [5]

classification: Small double-headed wooden hand drum (membranophone)
summary: A small double-headed wooden drum of the Raj Gonds of Adilabad, played with the fingers of both hands. It is one of the sacred Dandari drums, worshipped at the start of the festival, and gives its name to a lively Dandari dance.

about: The parra (also written para) is a small two-headed drum used by the Raj Gonds of the Adilabad region of northern Telangana, mainly in the Dandari festival season before Diwali [1][2]. Together with the gumela and vette drums and the kodal dance sticks it belongs to the set of Dandari instruments that are worshipped at the start of the festival [3][5].

It appears in a list of eighteen Gond instruments that, according to a 2013 account from Adilabad district, children learn at a traditional Gond learning centre called Gotul Pito [6]. The English Wikipedia describes the parra as a rhythm instrument used to keep the beat in the Gussadi dance [5].
construction: Haimendorf described para as small double-membrane drums that thicken slightly in the middle [1]. The Telugu writer Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy compares its shape with the maddela drum, gives its length as about two feet, and says both ends are covered with goat skin [2].

According to Haimendorf, a new para is carved from the wood of a kurm tree or, if none can be found, a vengun tree, because only the fine-grained wood of these two trees is considered suitable. The tree must have a natural hollow running up from its base, and the section containing this hollow becomes the drum shell. After felling, a piece of the trunk is carried to the village, where any experienced craftsman carves the shell; membranes of shaved and dried goat hide, or the skin of any wild animal, are stretched over both ends and held taut with criss-cross thongs of cow and goat hide [1].
playing: The para is played with the fingers of both hands. The player sits cross-legged and rests the drum against one knee [1][2]. Haimendorf described the 'small handy para, beaten caressingly with gentle fingers' at night-time dances in the rainy season [1].

In the Dandari ensemble each para goes with one or two vette (turbuli) drums [1]. Haimendorf heard 'the sharp rapid clicking of the turbuli and the deep tone of a para' give a quick, vivacious rhythm for a figure-of-eight dance of young men that was performed without singing [1].
cultural: Making a new para is a ritual act. Haimendorf recorded that, after the Akadi rite and before the Dandari season, a man from a family with the traditional right to keep a para goes to the forest with friends, a chicken and food offerings. He waves incense before the chosen tree and prays to the dance gods Dundria Raur and Sipiserma Raur for luck and the well-being of his children, marks the trunk with red powder (a line and as many dots as his clan has 'brothers'), and sacrifices the chicken so that its blood marks the bark. He offers the roasted liver and millet bread, throws grain into the branches and embraces the tree, first with the right and then with the left shoulder; the two men who will fell it do the same, and with each of the first six or seven axe strokes a wish is spoken, such as for good health, good harvests or more cattle [1].

Before a new para is played for the first time, a chicken is sacrificed in honour of Dundria Raur, patron of dance and song. The drums are sprinkled with water, vermilion and turmeric, a little vermilion powder is dropped into the small hole in the shell of a new para, and those present pray to the dance gods that the drums may sound well and that no harm may befall the dancers [1].

Ownership was inherited. Haimendorf wrote that anyone may play the dance drums but only men with a hereditary right could own a para or gumela, and that he knew of no man who owned both [1]. In a Dandari legend recited by Pardhan bards, the ancestors of the Raur clans resolve to make golden para drums and then take their para drums to the grandmother goddess Padmalpuri to dance the dance of greeting [1].

Today, on Bhogi, the first day of the Dandari festival, the parra is worshipped together with the gummela, vette and kodal before the Gussadi costumes are put on [3][5]. At the end of the festival, drums such as the gumela, parra and vette are put away until the next Akadi festival [4].
usage: The para accompanies Dandari dancing. Haimendorf wrote that one lively type of dance, more energetic than the dances to melodious gumela songs, 'is called para after the drum used in accompaniment', and his photographs include a boys' para dance [1].

Para drums are also played outside the festival itself: Haimendorf described boys gathering round fires at night with para and gumela drums before the first-fruits rite (Nowon), singing songs about the vegetables they could not yet eat [1].

The Dandari–Gussadi festival during which the parra is played is celebrated by Raj Gonds and Kolams in Adilabad, Kumuram Bheem Asifabad, Nirmal and Mancherial districts of Telangana and in neighbouring parts of Maharashtra [4].

classification: Reed wind instrument of the sannayi (shawm) type (aerophone)
summary: A shawm of the sannayi type played by the Pardhan musicians of the Raj Gonds in Adilabad. Played in pairs with the kikri fiddle and drums, it sounds at Gond clan-god rites, in the Dandari–Gussadi festival and at the Nagoba Jatara.

about: The pepre (also written pepri, pipri, pipre or pepera) is a wind instrument used in the ritual and festive music of the Raj Gonds of the Adilabad region of northern Telangana [3][4][5]. A Telugu account based on the book Mooladhwani describes the pepre as sannayi (shawm) instruments, two of which are played together with the kikri fiddle and a skin drum called dakki [2].

In his 1948 study of the Adilabad Gonds, Haimendorf illustrated the pepre and the bonga as 'Pardhan trumpets', noting that the two are usually played together, and he photographed Kanaka Ramu, a Pardhan of Pulera village, playing the pepre [1].
construction: Telugu sources place the pepre in the sannayi family [2], and the English Wikipedia describes it simply as a wind instrument that sounds like a flute or trumpet [4]. No detailed published account of its materials, making or makers was found during this research [2][4].
playing: The pepre is played in pairs. The Telugu account speaks of two pepre played together with the kikri and the dakki drum, and in Gond epic songs recorded by Haimendorf the phrase 'jora peprena' (a pair of pepre) is used when trumpets sound at a wedding [1][2].

Haimendorf wrote that at festivals the most prominent Pardhan usually plays the kingri fiddle while younger men blow trumpets and beat drums [1]. A 2013 list of eighteen Gond instruments from Adilabad district notes that the sanai, kikiri and kalikom are the instruments of the Pardhans [7].
cultural: A Gond origin myth recorded by Haimendorf explains why the Pardhans play wind instruments. When the culture hero Pahandi Kupar Lingal first organised the worship of the Gond gods, he asked the Gonds to play the fiddle, the trumpet and the drums. They refused to play fiddle and trumpet, saying that they would then be made to sit apart at feasts, so Lingal made a fiddle and a trumpet himself and the gods appointed Hirasuka as the first Pardhan to serve in the cult; then 'the Pardhan played fiddle and trumpet, and the Gonds beat the drums' [1].
Haimendorf also recorded another version, in which Hirasuka played only the fiddle and the Pardhans learnt to blow trumpets much later from musicians of the Mang caste [1].

Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy wrote that instruments such as the dappu, tudumu and pipre give energy to the Gusadi dance troupe, and that the Gonds regard the musical instruments and Gusadi dance equipment as highly sacred and worship them before the dance begins [8].
usage: Pardhan trumpets are heard at important moments of Gond religious rites. Haimendorf described 'the wail of Pardhan trumpets' breaking the stillness at first cock-crow on the day of a clan-god (Persa Pen) feast, trumpets and drums sounding as sacrifices were made, and Pardhans blowing trumpets beside the drummers at other village rites, where their role was purely that of musicians [1].

The pepre is among the instruments of the Dandari–Gussadi festival held around Diwali. It is listed with the dappu, tudumu and kalikom in Telugu and English accounts of the festival, and Village Square names the pepera among the instruments used in Gussadi celebrations [3][4][6][8].

At the Nagoba Jatara of the Mesram clan of Gonds at Keslapur, Indervelli mandal, the Deccan Chronicle reported in 2025 that the Adivasi instruments kalikom, dhol, thudum and pepri are played differently to suit each ritual or occasion [5].

traditions: Gond weddings (as described in Pardhan epics)

classification: Keyless side-blown (transverse) bamboo flute (edge-blown aerophone)
communities: Village cowherds and herders (as described in Telugu ballads and folk-arts surveys)
summary: The pillana grovi is the Telugu name for the simple bamboo flute, the instrument of Krishna. Village flutes of this kind were widely played in the Godavari region, and Telugu ballads describe herders playing them to call their calves.

about: Pillana grovi (also venuvu or murali) is the Telugu name for the bamboo flute. Telugu Wikipedia describes the venuvu, murali or pillanagrovi as a wind instrument made of well-dried bamboo, and the English Wikipedia article on the South Indian venu gives pillana grovi as its Telugu name. In 1891 C. R. Day recorded the bamboo flute of Southern India and the Deccan as the 'Pillagovi, or Murali'. [1][2][3]

The same simple instrument appears in village music and in classical music. The flute used in Carnatic concerts took its present form through 20th-century changes associated with Sarabha Sastri and T. R. Mahalingam. For the villages, Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy's survey of Telugu folk arts describes a short bamboo pillana grovi that was very widely played in the villages of the Godavari region and was loved by village people elsewhere as well. [1][2][4]
construction: The flute is made from well-seasoned bamboo. The tube is closed at one end and open at the other, with a blowing hole near the top. Below it are finger holes, which Telugu Wikipedia says number three in some flutes and eight in others. The quality of the sound depends partly on the bamboo used. [1]

The village flute described by Mikkilineni has one blowing hole and five small finger holes running from the middle to the far end, and is usually about 21 centimetres long. The classical venu is larger, with a blowing hole and eight closely placed finger holes, and is made in various sizes. [4][2]
playing: The player holds the flute sideways and blows across the blowing hole, using the fingers of both hands to close and open the finger holes. By overblowing and cross-fingering the classical flute reaches about two and a half octaves, and sliding the fingers on and off the holes produces the ornaments (gamakas) of Indian music. [2]

In the same survey, Mikkilineni describes another flute 'in use in many places in the Telugu country'. It is blown through a hole at one end and fingered with both hands, and is customarily played at weddings and other auspicious occasions and in leisure time. [4]
cultural: The flute is Krishna's instrument. C. R. Day noted that the pillagovi was traditionally believed to have been invented by Krishna, who is usually shown holding or playing it, and that the flute was held to be especially sacred. Telugu Wikipedia notes that Krishna is traditionally called venugana lola, 'the one who delights in the music of the flute'. [3][1]

The flute also belongs to the herding world of Telugu ballads. The Katamaraju Kathalu, the heroic ballad cycle of the Yadava (Golla) herders, describe the great herds setting out, 'playing pillanagrovis and calling the calves'. They also describe processions that move to tappeta drums, pillangrovis and horns. The texts were edited by Tangirala Venkata Subba Rao, largely from palm-leaf manuscripts kept by the traditional singers. [6]
usage: Besides everyday village playing in the Godavari region, Mikkilineni writes that in the Kakatiya period people blew pillana grovis while playing games and dancing the circular gondli dance during the Bathukamma and Boddemma festivals. [4][5]

In the Katamaraju ballads flutes are heard with drums and horns in the herders' processions. The same bamboo flute is also played in Carnatic music, where the venu took its present concert form in the 20th century. [6][2]

Tribal flutes (for example the Savara 'panar' and the flute called 'pirodi' used in peacock dances) are left to the tribal-instruments research.

classification: Double-reed wind instrument with a long conical wooden body and a flared bell (aerophone)
summary: Sannayi is the everyday Telugu name for the nadaswaram, the long double-reed pipe whose sound is considered auspicious. Played with the dolu drum, it accompanies weddings, temple rituals, village festivals and the Sankranti rounds of the Gangireddu bull performers.

about: In Telugu, the long double-reed pipe known in Carnatic music as the nadaswaram is usually called the sannayi. Telugu Wikipedia states that Telugu people call the nadaswaram 'sannayi', and C. P. Brown's Telugu–English dictionary of 1903 defines సన్నాయి as a kind of clarionet and gives నాగసరము (nagasaram) as its equivalent. J. P. L. Gwynn's modern dictionary glosses sannayi as a kind of clarinet and nadaswaram as an instrument similar to an oboe. Because these sources treat the two words as names for one instrument, this archive describes them on a single page. [1][2][3]

The nadaswaram is a double-reed instrument with a conical bore that widens towards the lower end, where it ends in a bell. It is among the loudest non-brass acoustic instruments and is best suited to open-air playing. In South Indian culture it is considered very auspicious: it belongs to the family of mangala vadyam ('auspicious instruments') and is heard at almost all Hindu weddings and in temples, including in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. [4][5]

Writing in 1891 about the music of Southern India and the Deccan, C. R. Day quoted Colonel Meadows Taylor's description of these pipes as the only regular outdoor instruments of Indian music. They were used at domestic and public religious ceremonies, processions, festivals and temple music, with different music for marriages, rejoicings, funerals, welcomings and departures. [6]
construction: C. R. Day described the nagasara as a reed pipe with a conical bore, usually pierced with twelve holes. Only the upper seven are fingered; the others are stopped with wax as the player chooses, to set the pitch. The reed, broad like a bassoon reed, is mounted on a short metal staple. The body was usually of a dark, close-grained wood with a metal bell, and spare reeds and an ivory pin for adjusting them hung from the pipe. [6]

Modern descriptions give the traditional body wood as aacha, although bamboo, sandalwood, copper, brass, ebony and ivory are also used. Old, seasoned wood is considered best, sometimes salvaged from demolished old houses. The reed (seevali) is made from a dried grass and sits in a small metal cylinder on a staple at the top. The pipe has seven finger holes plus five extra holes near the bottom that can be stopped with wax to change the tone, and a range of about two and a half octaves. Kamala Ganesh describes an instrument with an ebony body and a rosewood bell. [4][5]

The best-documented place where nadaswarams are made is Narasingampettai near Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu. There a few families turn the wood on lathes, drill the seven finger holes, smooth the body and fit the reed mouthpiece and the bell. The sources used for this page do not describe instrument makers in Andhra Pradesh or Telangana. [7]
playing: The reed at the top of the pipe is held between the player's lips. Fingering, breathing and tonguing all need great stamina and skill. Semitones and finer shades are produced by changing the pressure of the breath, and by only partly covering the holes. [4][5][6]

The sannayi is usually played in pairs with drums: the thavil, which Telugu Wikipedia equates with the dolu. A drone pipe (ottu or sruti) is tuned to the keynote. Telugu sources call the nadaswaram and dolu together the mangala vadyams, and the wedding band built around them is called a sannayi melam. [4][6][1]

In folk processions the sannayi plays fast, exciting music called veerangam. At Veerabhadra festivals and large jataras, Veerashaiva devotees perform a sword dance in front of decorated prabhas, with two or three groups of sannayi players walking ahead. The dolu drums beat very fast while the sannayis are blown at the highest pitch close to the sword-bearer's ears, rousing him to start the Daksha Yajna dandakam. [8]
cultural: Among Telugu Hindus the sannayi is tied to the barber-musician community now called Nayi Brahmin (listed with the names Mangali, Mangala and Bhajantri). Telugu Wikipedia notes that the community has long been known for its dolu and nadaswaram players, and links the name Mangala to the mangala vadyams they played. Edgar Thurston's survey of 1909 records that the Telugu barber caste Mangala took part in marriages 'by the melodious sounds of their flutes (nagasaram)'. It also records that at auspicious events a barber was called Bajantri, meaning musician, and that in the Vizagapatam district he was the village musician. [9][10][11]

A second hereditary tradition belongs to the Dudekula, a Telugu-speaking Muslim community. Sociologist Kamala Ganesh describes families of Muslim nadaswaram players in Guntur, Nellore, Vijayawada, Ongole and other places in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, many attached by hereditary right to local Hindu temples. A 1986 Telugu compendium by Bhusurapalle Venkateswarlu lists 107 Muslim players among 195 nadaswaram artists from the early 19th century onwards. It also names teaching centres (gurukulams) at Chilakaluripet, Guntur, Bandar, Kommuru, Rajahmundry and Kumkalagunta, supported by local zamindars and temples. [5][12]

Temple service carried hereditary rights. The family of Sheik Chinna Moulana of Karavadi in Prakasam district held the right to play at the village Rama temple through a land grant (manyam) from a local zamindar for about three centuries. A family member still plays for the deity there. [5][12]

The sannayi is also part of shared village festivals. Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy describes Pirla Panduga (Muharram) in Telugu villages: the pirs are carried through the village with a sannayi band and songs of mourning, and on the last night devotees carrying the pirs run through the fire pit amid loud sannayi and dappu music. [13]
usage: Weddings and temples remain the main settings. Among notable temple musicians, Gosaveedu Shaik Hassan (1928–2021) of Krishna district served as resident musician (asthana vidwan) of the Sita Ramachandraswamy temple at Bhadrachalam from 1950 to 1993. The Kasim–Babu brothers, grandsons of Sheik Chinna Moulana, have served as special nadaswaram artists of the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams. [14][15]

During the Sankranti season the Gangireddula performers go from house to house with a decorated bull. Their gear is described as a drone (sruti) and sannayi pipe, a dolu and a small bronze bell, and they play dolu and sannayi while singing folk songs and asking for alms. The bull is trained to move and bow to the music, and people consider it lucky when a Gangireddu stops at their door. In Visakhapatnam in 2025 the community was reported playing nadaswaram and drums. In 2026 V6 Velugu reported that fewer Gangireddu performers now come out in cities and villages alike: once seen all through January, they now appear only here and there, even on the three festival days. [16][17][18][19][20]

At Shaiva festivals and village jataras the sannayi leads the music. B. Ramaraju describes the Veeranatyam, danced by devotees at the Lingodbhava hour on Shivaratri, accompanied by the veeranam drum, dolu, tasha-marfa and sannayis. Mikkilineni describes goddess jataras in Krishna and Guntur districts, held after epidemics, that were celebrated with the veerangam of sannayi players and tappeta drums. At the yearly festival of the Palnadu heroes at Karempudi, he saw Perini dance movements performed before the heroes' images, driven by the veerangam of sannayis. [18][13][21]

Andhra Pradesh has produced leading concert players. Sheik Chinna Moulana (1924–1999) of Karavadi received the Padma Shri and the Madras Music Academy's Sangeetha Kalanidhi. The Andhra-born Sheik Mahaboob Subhani and his wife Kaleeshabi Mahaboob received the Padma Shri in 2020, and Kaleeshabi is described as the first Muslim woman to play the nadaswaram in public. Gosaveedu Shaik Hassan was awarded the Padma Shri after his death, in 2022. By the 1980s concert opportunities for the nadaswaram had begun to shrink, and in hereditary Muslim families many younger members now take up other work, although a few in each family still learn the instrument. [22][23][5][14][12]

Brown's 1903 dictionary (సన్నాయి = నాగసరము) and folk-arts books all use 'sannayi' for the nadaswaram-type pipe, so one page was made. C. R. Day (1891) also describes a smaller relative, the mukhavina, about half the size. The pipes carried by itinerant folk troupes may therefore be shorter than concert nadaswarams, but no source consulted describes a separate Telugu 'sannayi' distinct from the nadaswaram.

The sources disagree on materials and holes: Wikipedia gives aacha wood with 7 finger holes plus 5 wax-stopped holes; Day gives twelve holes (seven fingered) and a dark close-grained wood; Kamala Ganesh gives an ebony body with a rosewood bell.
No source consulted describes nadaswaram or reed makers in Andhra Pradesh or Telangana; the making process cited is from Narasingampettai, Tamil Nadu.

Telugu Wikipedia's articles on నాదస్వరం and నాయీ బ్రాహ్మణులు contain unsourced historical claims about the community's ancient origins; only the widely supported link between the community and dolu/nadaswaram playing is used here. The explanation of 'mangala vadyam' as 'instruments played by the Mangala people' is a folk etymology; Thurston links the name Mangala to 'mangalam' (auspiciousness).
Sheik Mahaboob Subhani's origin: Wikipedia says he was born in Prakasam district, while Kamala Ganesh (NCPA) says the family is originally from Satuluru in Guntur district.

Gangireddu troupes: the Deccan Chronicle (2025) says 'nadaswaram and drums', while Telugu sources say sannayi and dolu. This fits the two names referring to one instrument, but the exact pipes played by these troupes were not examined.

The Pirla Panduga, goddess-jatara, Veerabhadra and Perini descriptions come from Mikkilineni's 1992 book and may not reflect present-day practice. Thurston's 1909 survey uses colonial-era language and is used only for occupational facts.

classification: Concussion idiophone: a pair of small hand cymbals of bell metal, joined by a cord and struck together
summary: Talalu are small cymbals of bronze or other bell metal, joined by a cord and clashed together to mark the beat. They keep time in village bhajanas and in Telangana's Oggu Katha and Chindu Bhagavatam, and larger talalu ring out in forms such as the Kola Sambaram of the Godavari districts.

about: Talalu (singular talam) are a pair of metal cymbals struck against each other to keep rhythm. Telugu Wikipedia describes them as two bronze discs, also called manjira, jalra or gini, notes that the word is connected with clapping, and says that in Hindu devotional use they are also called karatalalu, 'hand cymbals' [1]. C. P. Brown's Telugu-English Dictionary (1903) gives tāḷamu both as 'time or measure in music' and as 'a cymbal, because used to keep time with', and records tāḷagiri for a cymbal player [2].

Because they mark the tala (rhythmic cycle), talalu appear in a very wide range of Telugu devotional and folk ensembles: seated bhajanas, dance bhajanas, Kolatam, and the long narrative performances of Telangana such as Oggu Katha [3][4][5].
construction: According to Telugu Wikipedia, talalu are made of bell metal, for which the article lists brass, bronze, copper, zinc and similar materials. A cord is tied through the hole in the middle of the cymbals, each cymbal is held together with its cord while playing, and the pitch of the sound depends on the size and weight of the cymbals [1]. Brown's dictionary likewise mentions the cymbal as a kanchu vadyamu, an instrument of bell metal [6].

Sizes vary between traditions. The talalu used in Oggu Katha are described as about twice the size of a palm, and smaller talalu are also used alongside them [4]. The Kola Sambaram storytellers of the Godavari districts use large talalu that give a loud sound [7], and Telangana Yadava storytellers of the Golla Suddulu tradition are described performing with a large drum and large talalu [8].
playing: The player holds one cymbal in each hand by its cord and strikes the pair together on the beats [1]. In an Oggu Katha troupe, which needs at least five members, the main narrator and his assistant stand in front and three musicians behind them play the dolu drum, the talam and the kanjira, also singing the chorus; the talam player takes up the kanjira when needed [4]. Mikkilineni notes that the talalu and dolu are played from the beginning to the end of an Oggu Katha performance [9], and Telugu Wikipedia lists rhythmic patterns used in Oggu Katha such as mendu talam, duyyara, adi talam and mendu bhairavi [4].
In the Chindu Bhagavatam troupes of Nizamabad district, the actors sing their own songs and verses while women of the troupe play the talalu; mridangam, harmonium and ankle bells are also used [10].

In the Kola Sambaram, a night-long storytelling performance about Lord Venkateswara, two men at the front swing burning torches (kolalu) while two singers at the back play large talalu and sing the refrain for the narrator [7]. In Adilabad district, Kolatam songs sung by elders are accompanied by harmonium and talalu [5].
cultural: Singing with talalu is a communal act of devotion. Mikkilineni describes villagers singing bhajanas together while sounding talalu in rhythm; energetic young men perform 'savamulla' bhajanas, which he explains as talala bhajanas (cymbal bhajanas) that involve dancing, while older men sit and sing Hari and Pandari bhajanas with hand cymbals and chirutalu. At Sri Rama Navami and Dasara, bhajana groups also stage plays in bhajana style through the night [3].

Oggu Katha, in which talalu are central, is a hereditary storytelling tradition of the Kuruma and Golla communities, who tell the stories of Beerappa and Mallanna. Telugu Wikipedia describes an 'Oggu deeksha' initiation: with the permission of caste elders, a trainee goes to a Shaiva shrine, meditates on Mallanna, receives a mantra and blessing from the Oggu elders and wears a necklace of seven cowries associated with Yellamma before becoming an Oggu performer [4]. Performances begin with praise of Ujjaini Mahankali followed by prayers to Ganapati and Sarada [9].

The Kola Sambaram with its large talalu is itself a devotional event: it is held at night on the day of deeparadhana by those who have returned from a pilgrimage to Tirupati, and tells a folk version of the love story of Venkateswara, Alamelu Manga and Bibi Nanchari; one of the performers becomes possessed during the performance, and in the past a bull was brought and set free afterwards [7].
usage: Talalu are used in Oggu Katha across Telangana [4][11], in Chindu Bhagavatam (Mikkilineni counted about fifty troupes in Nizamabad district) [10], and in the street plays of the Telaga Dasaris or Gante Bhagavatulu of Nalgonda, Khammam, Warangal and Hyderabad districts, where actors sing to harmonium, maddela and talalu [12]. Budige Jangams performing daytime pagati veshalu (disguise performances) go from house to house with harmonium, tabla and talalu [13].

In Karimnagar district, street plays (veedhi bhagotham) are accompanied by maddela, talam and harmonium [14]. Talalu also accompany Pandari bhajanas [15], Kolatam in Adilabad [5], and the Kola Sambaram, which is performed mostly in the East and West Godavari districts [7].

classification: Long-necked plucked string drone instrument carried on the shoulder (chordophone)
summary: The shoulder-held string drone of Telugu storytellers: the Burrakatha narrator plucks it while keeping time with metal rings (andelu), and the Sarada singers of Telangana call the same instrument 'Sarada'. It gave Burrakatha its name, from the burra or gourd shell of the tambura.

about: In Telugu folk storytelling the tambura (తంబుర, also written తంబురా or తంబూర) is the long-necked string instrument that the lead narrator (kathakudu) carries on the shoulder and plucks for the drone (sruti) while singing, dancing and telling the story [1][9]. It gave Burrakatha its name: the art form is said to be named after the burra, the gourd shell of the narrator's tambura, and the Telugu dictionaries Sabdaratnakaram and Suryarayandhra Nighantuvu explain the word tambura itself as tantri (string) plus burra [1][9][14].

The same instrument appears under local names in related traditions. The Sarada storytellers (Saradakandru) of Telangana call their shoulder tambura 'Sarada', a name of the goddess Saraswati, and a 1992 survey of Telugu folk arts states that it is no different from the tambura used in Burrakatha [1][2][15]. In the narratives of the Budiga Jangams, the lead singer's string instrument is called tambura and is also known as sarada or veena [10].
Because these sources treat them as one instrument, this page covers the Burrakatha tambura, the Sarada of the Sarada singers and the tambura of other wandering Telugu singers together [1][2][10].
construction: Folk tamburas are built on a hollow resonator. Writing on Burrakatha, S. Gangappa quotes a description of the narrator holding instruments such as the tambura or sarada made from the shell of a bottle gourd (sora burra) or a pumpkin (gummadi burra) [9]. Telugu Wikipedia distinguishes gourd-bodied tamburas with only one or two strings, used mostly by singers of tatvalu (philosophical songs) with just cymbals for accompaniment, from wooden tamburas with several strings used by Burrakatha narrators together with the gummeta drum [12].

Performers often make and decorate their own instruments. A 2011 account of the Sarada singers says that children of the community learn to make the sarada by hand, because village carpenters would not make instruments for a community treated as untouchable [11]. The Mala Jangams decorate their tambura with peacock feathers [4].

The narrator's kit is small and portable. For a Jangam katha or Burrakatha the narrator needs a tambura, three andelu (metal rings) and ankle bells for both legs, while the two accompanists need two gummeta drums; troupes carry their own instruments on their shoulders from village to village [1].
playing: The narrator holds the tambura on the shoulder and plucks its string for the drone, keeps time with andelu worn on the thumb or finger, and dances with bells on the ankles [1][3][9]. A Budiga Jangam narrator taps the rings against the tambura and plucks the string with the other hand, while a Sarada singer wears the andelu on his left thumb and plucks the tambura on his shoulder with his right hand [3][2]. One description adds that the Burrakatha narrator holds a second ring in the other hand and strikes the two together [16].

S. Gangappa describes the lead narrator plucking the tambura with one hand for sruti and keeping time with the other, on whose thumb he wears a ring (jantara) with a handkerchief-like piece of cloth tied to it; these rings are also called gumbeelu or andelu [9]. Mala Jangam narrators strike the gourd of the tambura with their finger rings in time with the story [4].

The tambura is seldom played alone. In Burrakatha two accompanists (vantalu) play gummeta drums, repeat the refrains and banter with the narrator, and in Sarada storytelling the narrator's wife or wives sing the refrain and play the dakki drum [1][2][11].
cultural: The name Sarada links the instrument to the goddess of learning. The Sarada singers named their tambura after Saraswati, begin their stories with a hymn to Sarada Devi, and sing refrains such as 'O Bharati, karunamati' and 'Bhali Sarada, karunanidhi' [2][15].

Sarada storytelling is a family occupation. Troupes are usually a husband with his wife or two wives, or other close relatives, who tour a fixed circuit of about forty villages called a patti. They are invited for marriages, harvests and festivals, and also at times of mourning, when they sing the life of the deceased and console the family [11][2].

According to the 1992 survey, the Saradakandru are Saivas whose gurus are Jangams, though they do not wear the linga, and they worship goddesses such as Yellamma and Pochamma [2]. The Jangam storytellers, whose tales spread Saivism, are said to have been singing them by about 1150 CE [1].

The Ganayata Jangams, who perform for a living, traditionally leave their settlements around Ashada (June–July), tour villages as performers and mendicants, and return home in Chaitra (March–April) for marriages and family events [10].

During Dhanurmasam, the month leading up to Sankranti, Haridasus go from house to house early in the morning with an akshaya patra (alms vessel) on the head, plucking a tambura on the shoulder, keeping time with chirutalu (clappers) and singing and dancing; they bless each household that offers rice [5].
usage: Burrakatha, performed in the villages of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, grew out of the older Jangam kathalu and is also called tambura katha, tandana katha or gummetla katha in different regions [1][16]. Its stories range from Palnati Veera Charitra, Bobbili Yuddham and Balanagamma to modern social and political themes, and twentieth-century narrators include Shaik Nazar [1].

Sarada kathalu belong to Telangana. The 1992 survey found most Sarada storytellers around Warangal, and the Sirishala family of Thondlayi village in Narketpally mandal, Nalgonda district, is known for the form [2][13]. Their stories include Sarvai Papadu, Sadasiva Reddy, Balanagamma, Bobbili and the Palnadu war, as well as a Sarada Ramayanam [2].

The tambura is also used by the Budiga Jangams, by the Mala Jangams (Panchalavaru), who tell Burrakatha-style stories through the night, and by the Pichhukuntla storytellers of Rayalaseema, who took up the tambura and gummetas under Jangam influence [3][4][6]. Haridasus at Sankranti, bhajana groups, and the Erukala fortune-teller (sodemma) also carry tamburas [5][7][8].

Patronage has declined. The 1992 survey noted that support for Sarada kathalu was shrinking day by day, and a 2011 account reported that schooling and other occupations were drawing young Sarada singers away from learning the ballads [2][11].

uncertain: One page or two: the 1992 Mikkilineni survey (Burrakatha and Saradakandru chapters), Telugu Wikipedia and the IJRAR paper all treat the Sarada and the Burrakatha tambura as the same instrument, so a separate 'burra' page was not made. No source describing a 'burra' instrument distinct from the tambura was found.

Construction is poorly documented. Gangappa quotes gourd or pumpkin shells; Telugu Wikipedia (unsourced) says Burrakatha tamburas are wooden with several strings while gourd tamburas with one or two strings belong to tatvalu singers; English Wikipedia says the shell may be baked clay, dried pumpkin, or brass and copper, but that sentence is marked 'citation needed'. The number of strings on Burrakatha or Sarada tamburas is not stated in a reliable source.

Etymology of 'burra': most sources derive it from the tambura's gourd; Mikkilineni also records a view that the gummeta drums were called burralu or dakkilu, which would give the same name; English Wikipedia's claim that burra means 'brain'/skull is unsourced.
Which hand wears the rings varies: left thumb for the Sarada singer (Mikkilineni), right thumb with a second ring in the other hand (English Wikipedia, citing a now-dead vepachedu.org page).

Telugu Wikipedia says Oggu katha narrators also use the tambura; the 1992 survey's Oggu katha chapter mentions only finger andelu (after a prayer to Sarada) and the form is named after the oggu drum, so this was not confirmed and is left out.

The same survey says the Telaga Dasarulu (Mittula Ayyavarlu) of Telangana have 'a kind of tambura' played with thin bells that gives both a tambura and a mridangam-like sound; this may be a different instrument (compare the Burra Veena and the kaddi vadyam) and is not described here.

Names of the Sarada singers vary: Saradakandru, Sarada Jangam, Saradagallu, Sarada Ganalu. Their origins are described differently: from Munnuru, Mutharasi and other Telugu castes (Mikkilineni, citing B. Ramaraju), or as an unrecognised Scheduled Caste sub-group registered as Jangam (Sphoorthi Theatre). The 2011 Sphoorthi account also places them in ten districts of Telangana, whereas the 1992 survey found them mainly around Warangal.
The claim that Jangam stories were sung by about 1150 CE is from the 1992 survey and was not checked against other historical sources.

summary: A small, flat, round drum tied to the chest and beaten with both hands by the dancers of Tappeta Gullu, the devotional dance of the Golla (Yadava) herding community of Srikakulam, Vizianagaram and Visakhapatnam in North Coastal Andhra. In everyday Telugu the word tappeta is also used for the dappu.

about: Tappeta (తప్పెట) is an old Telugu word for a drum. C. P. Brown's Telugu-English Dictionary (1903) defines both tappeta and dappu as 'a large drum', the Sabdaratnakaram (1912) explains dappu simply as 'tappeta', and G. N. Reddy's Telugu dictionary (1979) calls the dappu 'the tappeta used for making public announcements'. [1][2][3]

The two words are used for the same frame drum in different regions. The Telugu Akademi's regional dialect dictionary (2004) records tappeta and palaka as the Rayalaseema words for the dappu, and the Andhra Pradesh Sahitya Akademi's dialect dictionary (1970) records tappeta in the sense of dappu from Nellore, Kurnool, Telangana and Adilabad. The writer on folk arts Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy likewise writes that the dappu dance is also called tappetla vayidyam, and kanaka tappetlu in Rayalaseema, and that it is mostly played by the Madiga community. [1][2][4]

In North Coastal Andhra, however, the name is best known through Tappeta Gullu (తప్పెట గుళ్ళు), a dance in which every performer wears his own small drum on his chest, described by the Andhra Pradesh Shilparamam society as 'the Tappeta or gundlu, which is hung on the chest'. Mikkilineni describes it as a tappeta-like instrument made round out of metal sheet, tied on the chest and played vigorously with both hands. This page is about that chest drum. [5][6][7]

The word itself is Dravidian: the Dravidian Etymological Dictionary groups Telugu tappeṭa with Tamil tappaṭṭai and Kannada tappaṭe and tamaṭe, names for drums and tambourines. The Hans India explains the second half of the dance's name, gullu, as 'alarm', and repeats the local account that the drumming was once used by cowherds to keep wild animals away from grazing cattle. [8][9]
construction: Detailed descriptions of how the Tappeta Gullu drum is made are scarce. Mikkilineni's survey of Telugu folk arts, published by Telugu University in 1992, describes it as an instrument made round out of metal sheet (rēku), and the Telugu Wikipedia article on the dance repeats that the tappeta gunde is made round from metal sheet and tied over the chest. [6][7]
Other descriptions call it a flat drum, and Telugu dictionaries classify the tappeta in general as a charma vadyam, an instrument sounded on a stretched skin. [10][1]
playing: The drum is tied so that it hangs on the chest, leaving both hands free. Dancers beat it with both hands in changing rhythmic patterns (gatulu) while wearing ankle bells, moving in a circle, bending, rising and leaping, with shouts and long sung phrases. [6][10][11]

A troupe has a leader who is also its guru, and the whole performance follows his directions. Sources give troupe sizes of about 12 to 20 men, although a 2024 report describes a troupe of 30 to 35 artistes. [6][10][5][9]

As a performance builds up, the troupe splits into two groups that try to outdo each other with drum patterns and gamakas. At its height the dancers perform feats while still drumming: climbing onto one another to form a tower, two drummers hanging on either side of a third, or one man standing on the rim of a water-filled clay pot while another, standing on him, keeps drumming and dancing with a full pot of water on his head without spilling it. [6]

Besides leading the dancing, the leader narrates stories such as the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Bobbili war and sings kirtanas in between. Mikkilineni writes that a performance can last four to five hours and is given at night. [6]
cultural: Tappeta Gullu belongs above all to the Golla (Yadava) community, who keep herds of cattle, sheep and goats. Mikkilineni reports, citing Bittu Venkateswarlu, that when the rains fail and even fodder becomes scarce, Tappeta Gullu takes a prominent place in the worship offered to the gods for relief. The Andhra Pradesh Shilparamam society similarly describes the dance as performed by cowherds and shepherds since ancient times to please and propitiate Gangamma, the rain goddess, at village festivals held in her honour, with songs mostly in praise of Vishnu. [6][5]

The Yadavas worship Gangamma as their clan goddess and believe that Parvati was born as Gangamma, the wife of Katamaraju, at Shiva's command. Their origin story for the instrument says that Shiva gave away musical instruments to all the devotees who came to him, and gave the tappeta gullu that were left over to the Yadavas. [6][7]
When the dance is performed as a ritual, it begins with a man carrying a decorated pot of water around the village, a symbol of the rain goddess Gangamma. [10][11][12]

Mikkilineni records several customs around the art. Before performing in a village, a troupe accepts a token advance from the village elders, a quarter-rupee with a little jaggery, and fixes the date. Members work at their occupations by day and perform and practise at night, children are trained from a young age, and the performers are men. The performance is carried out with strict discipline, and any slip in its sequence is considered a disgrace. [6][9]
usage: The dance is practised mainly in Srikakulam, Vizianagaram and Visakhapatnam districts, and Mikkilineni also lists it among the folk arts of East Godavari. It is performed at jataras, at the Gapu sambaralu of the Golla community, at Gangadevi and village-goddess festivals and at Sri Rama koluvu, and is especially associated with Sankranti ('Pedda Panduga'). [6][13][7][9]

Its songs and ballads include the story of Gangamma, the Dasavataralu, Krishna leelalu, Sarangadhara charitra, Chenchita and Ammavari charitra, alongside local songs sung in the North Coastal Andhra dialect. [6][7][11]

In the early 1990s Mikkilineni found the art alive in Pallapeta and Muripella in Gajapathinagaram taluk of Vizianagaram district, under the leadership of Pellachina Narayana and Durla China Appalaswamy, with about forty villages around Gajapathinagaram having trained troupes, and at Sheru Mahammadpuram near Srikakulam under Kona Chinnavadu and later Korada Potappudu. In 2024 The Hans India profiled the Sri Krishna Tappeta Gullu troupe of Mudara Gollalapalem village (Padmanabham mandal), led by Allaboni Ramu and including third-generation performer Duvvu Shiva. Troupes have performed at Republic Day celebrations in Delhi and abroad, and the dance appears in the Telugu film Rangasthalam. [6][9][7]

Mikkilineni already described Tappeta Gullu in 1992 as surviving 'with its last breath' in scattered places and waiting for support. In 2024 troupe members told The Hans India that the younger generation had gradually lost interest, and asked the government for more opportunities to perform at temples, carnivals and major events. [6][9]
