uncertain: The sources consulted do not describe the playing face of the Tappeta Gullu drum or how it is fixed; Mikkilineni (1992) and Telugu Wikipedia only say the drum is made round from metal sheet. A claim on some websites that it is a cone of tin or wood covered with leather could not be traced to a source that could be read.

Name overlap with the dappu: dictionaries treat tappeta and dappu as the same frame drum (tappeta being the Rayalaseema word), while the Tappeta Gullu chest drum is a smaller, different instrument. This page covers the chest drum; the general frame drum belongs on the Dappu page. The Dravidian Etymological Dictionary lists tappeṭa but a search for ḍappu found no entry, so any historical link between the two words is not established here.

The explanation of 'gullu' as 'alarm' and the story that the dance began as a way to scare off wild animals come from a newspaper report and look like local explanations; they are not confirmed by scholarly sources.
Troupe sizes vary between sources: 12 to 15 (Jai Ho Srikakulam), 12 to 20 (Auchitya), up to about 20 (Mikkilineni) and 30 to 35 (The Hans India, 2024).

Telugu Wikipedia (without a cited source) credits a 19th-century Srikakulam poet, Balivada Narayana, with the first Tappeta Gullu ballad, 'Sri Krishna', and names the Korrayi Gangayya and Duryodhana brothers of Gollapeta (Pathapatnam mandal) as keepers of the art. These claims were not confirmed elsewhere.

Telugu Traditions and Telugu Wikipedia say the tradition is about 400 years old (Telugu Traditions traces its origin to Srikakulam district); neither gives a source for this figure, so it is not used in the text.

about: Tudumu (తుడుము) is an old Telugu word for a drum. Dictionaries gloss it as 'a kind of drum' or 'tom-tom' (Brown's dictionary also gives tudumuvadu, 'a drummer'), and the Sabdaratnakaram (1912) cites it from a verse of the Accha Telugu Ramayanam that names bugles (buralu) and tudumus together. [1][2]

Several dictionary entries point to a kettle drum. The Andhra Pradesh Sahitya Akademi's dialect dictionary (1970) defines tudumu as a small nagara (kettle drum) played with leather strips, recorded from Nellore and Warangal, with the example 'they announced it with the tudumu'. The Telugu Akademi's regional dictionary (2004) gives tudumu as the North Coastal Andhra (Kalinga) dialect word for the drum called ḍhaṅkā, and G. N. Reddy's dictionary of synonyms (1990) lists kadavateetu and gummeta as its synonyms. [1]

The word is shared with neighbouring tribal languages. The Dravidian Etymological Dictionary records Telugu tuḍumu 'a kind of drum, tomtom' with Gondi tuḍum 'drum' (and turam 'kettle drum' in Grigson's Gondi vocabulary) and Kui ṭuḍumi 'a kind of drum', and compares Marathi tuḍūm, a kind of kettle-drum. [3]
construction: M. A. Rauf, writing on tribal musical instruments as part of the documentation work of the state's Tribal Cultural Research and Training Institute, and quoted by Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy, describes the tudumu as an instrument made of clay in a hemispherical shape. Goat skin is stretched tightly over the top, and leather straps running over the rim of the hemisphere hold the skin taut. [4]
playing: The drum is set on a ring of rope and beaten with leather straps, a method also recorded in the 1970 dialect dictionary's definition of the tudumu as a small kettle drum played with leather strips. [4][1]

In the Araku valley, the Dhimsa dance moves to an ensemble of tundi, mori, kiridi, tudumu and dappu, and pairs of horns (jodu kommu) are blown now and then to excite the dancers; a 2024 report likewise names the dappu, tudumu, mori, kiridi and jodukommu as the instruments that give Dhimsa its rhythm. [5][6]
cultural: Among the Raj Gonds of Adilabad, the instruments of the Gussadi dance, including the dappu, tudumu, pipre, baka and kalikoy, are considered sacred, and they are worshipped before the dance begins. Telangana Today reported in 2025 that Raj Gonds and Kolams mark the start of the dance season by worshipping peacock-feather crowns and the musical instruments used by the dance troupes. [7][8]

The Hans India reported in 2021 that during Dandari-Gussadi the Gonds and Kolams revere the goddess Jangubai by playing dappu, ghumela, dhol, vetti, karra and 'thudem' before the deity, and that these instruments are now almost extinct from the markets. [9]

In the Araku valley, Dhimsa is danced at the Chaitra festival (also called itela panduga, the festival of spears), at weddings and on festival days. One form, Bode Dhimsa, is danced during the worship of the village goddess Nisani Devata and begins with all the instruments playing loudly. [5]
usage: Rauf notes that the tudumu is used mainly in Dhimsa dances and that the Samantha tribe and the Gonds use it most. [4]

Dhimsa is performed by communities of the Araku valley in the Visakhapatnam agency, where Mikkilineni names the Valmiki, Bagata, Kondadora and Kotia among the main tribes. A 2024 Deccan Chronicle report on Dhimsa dancers from the agency areas along the Andhra Pradesh-Odisha border, naming dancer Korra Dhana Lakshmi and troupe leader Pangi Arjun, says a traditional performance needs at least eight women and six men, and that the dancers were seeking recognition as artists. [5][6]
In Telangana the tudumu is part of the Gussadi and Dandari dances of the Raj Gonds of Adilabad, held around Diwali. [7][9]

uncertain: The detailed physical description (hemispherical clay body, goat skin, leather straps, played on a rope ring) comes from a single account, M. A. Rauf's, as quoted by Mikkilineni (1992). It fits the dictionary definition of tudumu as a small kettle drum played with leather strips, but it was not confirmed by fieldwork photographs or other ethnographic sources.

It is not confirmed that the drum called 'thudem' or 'tudum' by the Gonds of Adilabad today is the same clay kettle drum Rauf describes. Photographs published by Telangana's Department of Language and Culture with 'Tudum' in the file title show a large cylindrical drum played with sticks, which does not match Rauf's description.

Some websites (including an AI-generated encyclopedia) describe the tudumu as a cylindrical drum of tamarind or neem wood with goat or buffalo hide; this is not supported by any source read and conflicts with the dictionary and Rauf descriptions.
Use of the tudumu by the Koya tribe could not be confirmed: sources on the Koya Kommu Koya dance name their drum dolu.
Dictionaries overlap: G. N. Reddy (1979) also glosses tudumu as 'tappeta', and the Sabdaratnakaram glosses gummeta as 'tudumu', so the word has been used loosely for several kinds of drum.
The 'Samantha' tribe is named as in Mikkilineni's Telugu text (సామంత జాతి); the modern English name of this community was not checked.
Mikkilineni's chapter on the Mala Jangalu mentions a 'tudum kommu'; it is unclear whether this is a drum, a horn or a combination.

classification: Small saucer-shaped single-headed drum (membranophone), played with two sticks
summary: A small, shallow drum of the Raj Gonds of Adilabad, made from a clay, iron or wooden bowl covered with skin and struck with two thin bamboo sticks. One of the Dandari festival drums, it gives a sharp, clicking rhythm; according to a Gond legend and a custom recorded in the 1940s, a new vette is touched by a menstruating woman so that it sounds right.

about: The vette (also written wete or vetti) or turbuli is a small single-headed drum with a shallow, saucer-shaped shell. It is used by the Raj Gonds of the Adilabad region of northern Telangana during the Dandari festival season before Diwali [1][2][3].

It belongs to the group of Dandari dance drums together with the parra and the gumela: Haimendorf noted that each para, and each pair of gumela, is accompanied by one or two vette drums [1]. At the start of the festival the vette is worshipped along with the gummela, parra and kodal dance sticks [4][6].
construction: Haimendorf described turbuli, also known as wete, as saucer-shaped single-membrane drums made of wood, burnt clay or iron, usually not more than ten inches in diameter [1]. Mikkilineni Radhakrishna Murthy's Telugu account says the Gonds of Adilabad make its plate-like shell from potter's clay, iron or wood and stretch skin over it, but gives the diameter of the skin as usually more than ten inches [2].

Although the legend speaks of wooden turbuli, Haimendorf found that Gonds in the 1940s used earthen ones, buying the clay bowl called werni from local potters, or similar iron shells made by a blacksmith [1]. When buying a wete from a potter the buyer gave a chicken, some grain and often cash, and the goat-skin membrane was attached with iron hoops and leather thongs [1].
playing: The vette is beaten with two slender splinters of bamboo [1]. Mikkilineni likewise says it is played with two thin sticks [2].

Its sound is sharp and quick. Haimendorf described how 'the sharp rapid clicking of the turbuli and the deep tone of a para' gave a lively rhythm for a Dandari dance of young men performed without songs, and he saw a visiting Dandari troupe arrive with earthen turbuli hung on their shoulders [1].
cultural: A Dandari legend recited by the Pardhan bards explains a striking custom. The Raur ancestors made para drums, and also turbuli from kursi wood, but the turbuli would not sound true. They asked the wise Pardhan Hirasuka, who said that the Gond gods were unruly and could not be controlled, and advised that the drums be touched by a menstruating woman, and that new shells be bought from the potter and covered with hide. When a menstruating woman touched them, the drums sounded well [1].

Haimendorf found the custom still followed in the 1940s: every new wete drum was touched by a menstruating woman, following the advice attributed to Hirasuka. He pointed out that this is remarkable because menstruating women were otherwise thought to defile ritual objects and were kept away from ceremonies, and suggested that the idea may be to neutralise one evil with another [1].

As with the other Dandari drums, the first playing of a new wete must be preceded by a chicken sacrifice in honour of Dundria Raur, the patron of dance and song, at which the drums are sprinkled with water, vermilion, turmeric and the sacrificial blood [1].

Today, on Bhogi, the first day of Dandari, the vette is worshipped together with the gummela, parra and kodal before the Gussadi costumes are put on, and at the end of the festival drums such as the gumela, parra and vette are put away until the next Akadi festival [4][5].
usage: The vette is played during the Dandari–Gussadi festival in the Gond villages of Adilabad, Kumuram Bheem Asifabad and parts of Mancherial and Nirmal districts. The Hans India lists the vetti among the Dandari instruments, alongside the dappu, ghumela, dhol, karra and tudum [3].

In Haimendorf's account the para and turbuli accompanied the dances of the Dandari troupe, while the dance of the masked Gussadi performers was accompanied instead by the large dapna drums and kettle-drums [1].
In 2021 The Hans India reported that these Dandari instruments were almost extinct from the markets [3].

uncertain: Names: vette (Telugu Wikipedia, Mikkilineni), wete and turbuli (Haimendorf), vetti (The Hans India), turubuli (తురుబులి, Mikkilineni). All appear to refer to the same drum; Haimendorf explicitly says turbuli are also known as wete.
Diameter: Haimendorf says usually not more than ten inches, Mikkilineni says usually more than ten inches.

In the English translation of the Dandari legend in Haimendorf's book, the Gondi word turburi is rendered 'kettle-drums', although elsewhere he treats turbuli and the iron kettle-drum as different drums.
The menstruation custom and the purchase details come from fieldwork in the 1940s; no recent source confirming whether the custom continues was found.
'Karra' in The Hans India list is probably the dance sticks rather than a drum; not confirmed.
